Surat al-Zukhruf (The Adornment)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ha Mim﴾. The discussion concerning it follows the manner already mentioned at the opening of Ya Sin.

﴿By the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an, and what is meant by it is all of it. It is permitted that what is meant is its genus, which is true of some of it and of all of it. It was also said: it is permissible that what is meant is the genus of the revealed books, or what is written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), or the verbal noun meaning writing and inscription. God, glorified is He, swore by it because of its great benefits, and the deficiency in this is not hidden. The preferable view, on the assumption that (Ha Mim) is a noun, is that it is a name for the Qur'an, and that the Book is also meant by this, and it is sworn by either as a fresh beginning or by conjunction with (Ha Mim) on the assumption that it is in the genitive by the implied particle of oath. This is on the basis that the ground of conjunction is difference in designation. However, this requires the omission of the genitive particle while its government remains, as in:

Kulayb pointed with the fingers of their palms (ashaarat Kulayb bil-akuff al-asabi')

The prohibition of swearing by two things with a single particle is not to be heeded. The basis for repeating the oath is emphasis on the oath clause.

﴿The Clear﴾, that is, clear to those to whom it was revealed, because it is in their language and according to the styles of their speech; this is on the basis that it is from abana (intransitive, to be clear). Or, it means clarifying the path of guidance from the path of error, making clear the fundamentals of what is needed in matters of religion; this is on the basis that it is from abana (transitive).

﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is the answer to the oath. The verb *ja'l* (making) here carries the sense of *taṣyīr* (rendering or making something into a state), and it takes two objects. It does not carry the sense of *khalq* (creating), which takes one object. This is not because the latter would contradict the exaltation of the Qur'an. Rather, it is because the sense of the context under discussion (*dhawq al-maqām*, the discerning sense of the situation) rejects it. The speech was not brought to emphasise that the Qur'an is created, and the disbelievers' denial was not directed at that. Rather, the verse is driven toward establishing that it is a Qur'an in Arabic, clearly explained, revealed in their own modes of expression, such that understanding what is in it, and perceiving that it is miraculous, is not difficult for them. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may reason﴾, meaning, so that you may understand it, comprehend the lucid insight and the sublime meanings within it, become aware of the testimonies it contains that bear witness to its being beyond the capacity of humans, recognise the true blessing in that, and that your excuses be completely cut off. Swearing by the Qur'an for this purpose is one of the fine and original forms of oath, because it observes correspondence, and it alerts to the fact that nothing is higher than it, such that one would swear by something else, and nothing is more important than describing it, such that one would swear concerning it. As Abu Tammam said:

*And by your front teeth, indeed they are Ighriḍ (fresh and bright),*
*and by the lustre of a people and the glimmer of lightning.*

On the basis that the answer to the oath is his saying: "indeed they are Ighriḍ."

The verse has been cited as evidence that the Qur'an is created, and they extended the discussion on this. It was answered that even if it indicates createdness, it does not indicate more than the createdness of verbal speech (*al-kalām al-lafẓī*), and there is no dispute about that.

You know that the Hanbalites (*al-Ḥanābila*) dispute this, and they have answers to the argument mentioned in their books. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Tawus, who said: A man from Hadramawt came to Ibn Abbas and said to him: "O son of Abbas, tell me about the Qur'an: is it speech from the speech of God, the Exalted, or a creation from the creation of God, glorified is He?" He said: "Rather, it is speech from the speech of God, the Exalted. Have you not heard God, glorified is He, say: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection until he hears the speech of God﴾?" The man said to him: "What then of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾?" He said: "God, the Exalted, wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ*) in Arabic. Have you not heard God, the Exalted, say: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a Preserved Tablet﴾? So reflect on it."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 43, verse 4:

﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ — that is, in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*), according to what a group of scholars has held, for it is the source of all the heavenly books, meaning their origin, because they are all transcribed from it. It has also been said that "the Mother of the Book" is the eternal knowledge. It has been said too that it refers to the clear verses (*al-ayat al-muhkamat*), and the pronoun refers either to the Book in the sense of the surah, meaning that it is contained in the clear verses which are the "Mother," and this, as you see, is weak.

The two brothers (*al-Akhawan*) read *Imm* with a kasra on the hamza, to follow the kasra on the mim, or [they read] *al-Kitab* so that the kasra is not applied when not connected. ﴿With Us﴾ — that is, in Our presence; ﴿exalted﴾ — of high rank among the books, because of its inimitability (*i'jaz*) and its containing great secrets; ﴿full of wisdom﴾ — possessing perfect wisdom, or firmly established so that no other can abrogate it (*naskh*), or ruling over the other books. These two are predicates of *inna*. Regarding ﴿in the Mother of the Book﴾, it has been said that it is connected to ﴿exalted﴾, and the *lam* (of *la'ali*), since it has been detached from its position and changed from its original form, has lost its right to initial position, so it is permissible to place what falls within its scope before it. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it, since it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun that precedes it, or from its concealed pronoun. And ﴿with Us﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿in the Mother of the Book﴾. Although the two differ in meaning, they agree in what they result in. Or it is a circumstantial clause from it, or from *al-Kitab*, since the noun in the genitive construction is treated as part of the whole, because it may be dropped. Perhaps the preferred view is that the two adverbial phrases are in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a resumption explaining the position of the ruling, as if it were said after explaining its being characterized by the two sublime qualities mentioned: "This is in the Mother of the Book and with Us." They did not permit their being in the position of the predicate of *inna*, because the *lam* enters on something other than them.

Whatever the case, the emphasized sentence is either a coordination with the sentence sworn upon, falling under its ruling, or a resumed sentence confirming the exalted status of the Qur'an, which the oath indicated in the manner of a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if only you knew﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 43, verse 5:

After Allah, glorified is He, had shown the great exalted status of the Qur'an, and had established that its being sent down in their language was so that they might understand it, believe in it, and act in accordance with what it requires, He followed that by denying that the matter could be the opposite of this. So He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿Shall We then withhold the Reminder from you altogether﴾. That is, shall We push it away and remove it from you, by way of allegorical metaphor (*istiʿarah tamthiliyyah*, a metaphor built on a whole scene), from the saying: "He drove the strays away from the watering-place" (*darab al-gharaʾib ʿan al-hawd*). He likened the state of the Reminder and its removal to the state of strayed camels being driven away from the watering-place when they enter among others at the time of watering. Then he used for this case what was in that story. This implies that wisdom requires the Reminder to be directed towards them and to remain with them, as if it were pressing upon them. Had it been taken as a metaphor in a single word, making "withholding" equal to "striking", it would also be permissible. Among this is the verse of Tarafah:

*I shall strike away from you the cares that come upon you,*
*as you strike the forehead of the horse with the sword.*

And the words of al-Hajjaj in his sermon threatening the people of Iraq: "I shall strike you with the strike of strayed camels." As for *al-dhikr* ("the Reminder"), it was said that it means the Qur'an, and this is related from al-Dahhak and Abu Salih. The speech is then on the assumption of an elided noun, that is, "the sending down of the Reminder," and in this there is the use of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, for glorification. It was also said: rather, it is the Reminder of the servants with what is good for them, so it is in the sense of a verbal noun in its literal meaning. And from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid: what it requires.

The interrogative *hamzah* is for denial, and the *fa'* is for conjunction, coordinating with an elided element that it requires, according to one of the two opinions regarding this type of construction. That is, "Shall We then neglect you, and withhold the Reminder from you?" Ibn al-Hajib said: the *fa'* is to explain what precedes it, and what precedes it is that making the Qur'an Arabic is the cause of what follows, and what follows is the denial that Allah, glorified is He, would withhold the Reminder from them. ﴿Altogether﴾ means, that is, by turning away (*iʿrad*). It is a verbal noun (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of *nadribu* but not from its own root, since removing the Reminder is a turning away. Its accusative case is as an absolute object, on the pattern of "I sat in a sitting" (*qaʿadtu juluusan*). It is as if it were said: "Shall We then turn away from you in turning away?" Or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿul lahu*), or as a circumstantial state (*hal*) interpreted as *musafihin*, meaning "turning away." The root meaning of *safh* is that you turn the thing to the side of your neck. It was also said that it has the meaning of "side," so it takes the accusative of place (*zarf*), meaning: "Shall We remove it from you to one side?" This is supported by the reading of Hassan ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Dabʿi, al-Sumayt ibn ʿUmayr and Shubayl ibn ʿUdhrah, *ṣufḥan* with a *ḍammah* on the *ṣad*. In that case it may be that the form is a lightened *ṣufḥ*, like *rusul*, as the plural of *ṣafūḥ* in the sense of "turning away." Abu Hayyan preferred that it be singular, in the sense of "opened," like *al-sadd* and *al-sudd*.

It is related from Ibn ʿAtiyyah that the accusative of *ṣafḥan* is as a verbal noun emphasising the content of the preceding sentence, so that the governing verb is elided. It is not hidden that this does not clearly appear. In any case, the meaning is the denial that the matter could be contrary to what was mentioned, namely the sending down of a Book in their language so that they might understand it. ﴿Because you are a people who exceed the limits﴾. That is, "because you are people immersed in excess and persisting in it," meaning that wisdom requires that you be remembered and that the Qur'an be sent down to you, so We do not abandon that because you are excessive, not paying attention to it. Rather We act, whether you pay attention or not.

It was also said: the meaning is that your state, although it would require that you be left to your own devices until you die in disbelief and error and remain in everlasting punishment, nevertheless, out of the vastness of Our mercy, We do not do that. Rather We guide you to the truth by sending the trustworthy Messenger and sending down the clear Book.

Nafiʿ and the two brothers (*al-Akhawan*) read *in kuntum* with a *kasrah* on the *hamzah*, so that the clause is conditional (*shartiyyah*). *In* is used for what is doubtful, and their excess is a established matter. But it is used here on the basis of treating the addressee as if he were hesitant about the occurrence of the condition, doubting it, with the aim of attributing to him ignorance in committing excess, presenting it as the form of something whose non-existence is required and which could not come from one who reasons. It was also said: there is no need for this, because the condition is excess in the future, and this is not certain. This was refuted by saying that *in* when attached to *kana* does not turn it to the future, according to most grammarians. For this reason it was said: *in* here means *idh* ("since"). It was supported by the fact that ʿAli ibn Zayd read with it, and that it indicates causation, so it agrees in meaning with the reading with *fath*. Even if this is granted, what is apparent from the state of the persistent excessive person is that he remains as he is, so it is certain in the future as well, on the view that *in* turns *kana* just as other verbs do. The answer to the condition is elided, relying on what precedes as an indication of it. It was also allowed that the condition is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning "your excess being supposed," in the sense of an equitable speech, so no answer needs to be posited.

It was objected that this works only on the view that the conjunctive *in* occurs in their speech without a *waw*, whereas what is known in Arabic is the opposite.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾, is another kind of consolation for him (ﷺ). The pronoun in ﴿them﴾ refers to the transgressors being addressed, not to that to which the pronoun in "(what came to them)" refers, on account of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the example of the former peoples has passed on﴾, meaning: their story has already been mentioned more than once in the Qur'an, a story which by right should become a proverb (mathal).

The word ﴿might﴾ (batshan) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It has also been permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of ﴿We destroyed﴾, meaning: "while they were exercising might." The first is better. He described those (former peoples) with greater strength in order to establish the ruling on these (addressees) by way of a stronger argument (al-awlawiyyah).

Al-Alusi's commentary on verse 9 of surah 43:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the preceding address, and the two verses, namely His saying ﴿How many a prophet We sent﴾, form a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) to convey affirmation (taqrir) and consolation (tasliyah), as you have heard. The meaning is: if you asked them who created the world, they would ascribe its creation to one who is characterized by these attributes in reality, not that they would utter these words and describe Him, exalted is He, with the attributes mentioned. This is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, as attributed to him. This is good, and it has a parallel in common usage: if someone informed you that the Shaykh said such-and-such, meaning by "the Shaykh" Shams al-Aʾimmah, and then you met Shams al-Aʾimmah and said, "So-and-so informed me that Shams al-Aʾimmah said such-and-such," even though so-and-so had not uttered anything but "the Shaykh," yet you mention his titles and attributes. Likewise here, the disbelievers say, "God created them," and do not deny it. Then God, mighty and majestic, mentioned His attributes, i.e., that God, exalted is He, to whom they attribute the creation of the heavens and the earth, possesses such-and-such attributes, may He be glorified.

Ibn al-Munir said: ﴿the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ is part of the speech of those being questioned, and what follows is His speech, may He be glorified. In al-Kashshaf it is said that there is no difference between this view and this one in substance, for it is a report of speech from them, connected to His speech, on the basis that it is part of His speech, even if they had not actually uttered it. This is like when your interlocutor says, "Zayd honored me," and you say, "He who honored you and greeted you," or to other people present, "He who honored you and greeted you," where you connect his speech as if it were part of it, but you do not make it part of his quoted words.

The more apparent view in terms of wording is what Ibn al-Munir mentioned. In that case, an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) occurs in ﴿and We revived﴾ after its place. A parallel to this is His saying, reported from Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾, up to His saying: ﴿and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾. Repeating the verb in the answer shows concern for its matter, and its correspondence to the question is in meaning, according to what Abu Hayyan claimed, not in wording. He said: because "man" is a subject (mubtadaʾ), if it corresponded in wording it would have been with a noun as subject, not with a verb, by saying: "The All-Mighty, the All-Knowing created them."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 10:

﴿The One who made the earth for you a cradle﴾: a place made smooth, that is, spread out and made level, its outcome being that it is spread out for you so that you may settle in it. This does not contradict its being spherical (kuriyyatuha) due to the greatness of its size. It is narrated from Asim that he recited (mahdan) without an alif.

﴿And made for you therein roads (subul), paths that you traverse on your journeys, so that you may be guided﴾: that is, so that you may be guided by travelling them to your destinations, or by reflecting upon them to tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), which is the primary aim.

﴿And who sent down water from the sky in measure﴾: that is, in a measure required by the will, which is founded upon wisdom and benefit. No one knows the exact quantity of what is sent down of that each year with certainty except God, Exalted and Majestic. As for the instrument the philosophers have made in these eras, called the odometer (al-udumitir), by which they claim the amount of rain falling in every country throughout the entire year can be known, it does not yield certainty even for one small locality, let alone others, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

And in al-Bahr (al-Muhit) it is said: "in measure" means by decree and determination from eternity. The first (interpretation) is preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 11:

﴿So We revived thereby﴾, i.e., We gave life by that water ﴿a land dead﴾, wholly devoid of growth and vegetation.

Abu Ja'far and Isa read (maytan) with the doubled letter (shaddah), and its masculine form is because al-balda is in the sense of al-balad and al-makan (the place). Al-Jalabi said: It is not far, and Allah the Exalted knows best, that the feminine of al-balad and the masculine of ﴿maytan﴾ indicate that the state of its weakness has reached its utmost limit. In the statement there is a metaphor, either implicit (makniyyah) or explicit (tasrihiyyah).

The shift (iltifat) in (anshharna) to the plural "We" of majesty (nun al-'azamah) serves to show the perfection of concern with the matter of giving life and to indicate the greatness of its importance. ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that "shar" (reviving) which in reality is bringing forth from the earth, and it is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), i.e., a reviving such as that. ﴿You will be brought forth﴾, i.e., you will be raised from your graves alive. In expressing the bringing forth of plants by the "shar" which is the giving of life to the dead, and expressing their giving of life by "bringing forth," there is an exaltation of the status of plant-growth and a belittling of the matter of resurrection, and in that there is what there is of refutation of those who deny it.

Ibn Wththab, Abdullah ibn Jubayr, Isa, Ibn Amir, and the two brothers (al-akhawan) read (takhrujun) with the verb in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il).

﴿Who created all the pairs﴾, that is, the kinds of created things. Here "zawj" (pair) means "kind" (ṣinf), not its well-known meaning. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "al-azwāj" means the varieties and types, such as sweet and sour, white and black, and male and female. It has also been said that everything other than Allah, glorified is He, is a zawj, because it cannot be free of an opposite, such as above and below, right and left, past and future, and so on. The one that is free of an opposite is Allah, mighty and majestic. It has been objected that the claim that this applies to all existing things without exception is not free from scrutiny.

Perhaps whoever said "everything other than Allah, glorified is He, is a zawj" did not base the matter on what was mentioned, but based it on the principle that the Necessary Existent, majestic is His state, is one in every respect, with no composition in Him, glorified is He, in any way, neither mentally nor externally, and likewise no possible existent, whether material or immaterial, is so.

﴿And He made for you, of the ships and the livestock, that which you ride﴾, that is, that which you ride upon. Here "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) and its returning pronoun (ʿāʾid, the pronoun referring back to the antecedent) is omitted. Riding, with regard to the ship, is transitive through a particle, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they board the ship﴾. It is different with regard to the animal, for it is transitive directly, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿that you may ride them﴾. However, the form transitive without an intermediary has prevailed because of its strength over the form transitive through an intermediary. So the figurative usage required by this prevalence is with regard to the object of the verb. Or, the created thing (the animal) has prevailed for riding over that which is made for it (the ship), because it is the creation of the Creator, the All-Powerful. Or, the more common usage has prevailed over the rare. So the figurative usage lies in "mā" and its pronoun, to which riding is directly transitive, not in the relation to the object. And it is for the prioritization (taghlīb) of the animal that is ridden over the ship.

[Page 68]

﴿So that you may settle upon their backs﴾. Here he expressed the act of settling on all of them by "settling upon the backs" specifically of beasts. The pronoun refers to "that which you ride." The singular ظهر (*zahr*, "back") is used out of regard for the wording, and the plural ظهور (*zuhur*) is used with its pronominal suffix out of regard for the meaning. The apparent reading is that the lam in ﴿لِتَسْتَوُوا﴾ (*li-tastawu*) is the lam of purpose (*lam kay*, "lam of purpose"). Al-Hawfi said: "Whoever affirms the lam of result (*lam al-sayrura*, "lam of consequence") may hold that it applies here too." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is the lam of command (*lam al-amr*, "imperative lam"). But this is distant, since it would require addressing the second person with the second-person prefix. Its use as a command to the addressee has been disputed. It has been said that this is a poor, rare dialect, found hardly ever except in an irregular reading, such as ﴿فَبِذَلِكَ فَلْتَفْرَحُوا﴾ ("So let them rejoice in that"), or in poetry, such as his saying:

"Stand up, you, O son of the best of Quraysh."

As for what the traditionists have reported from his saying, peace be upon him: "Let your rows be taken up" (*li-ta'khudhu masaffakum*), it may be a narration by meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a good dialect. Abu Hayyan followed the first view and attributed it to the majority of the grammarians.

﴿Then you may remember the blessing of your Lord when you have settled upon it﴾. That is, that you remember it in your hearts, acknowledging it and regarding it as great, and then you praise Him for it with your tongues. This is the meaning of remembering Allah's blessing upon them, according to what al-Zamakhshari said. The sum of it is that remembrance includes the stirring of the heart and passing over the tongue, so it is understood in its most complete state, which is remembrance by the tongue together with awareness from the heart. As for acknowledgment and magnifying, these come from "the blessing of your Lord," since it requires bringing it to mind in the heart. This is exactly the praise which is thankfulness in this context, not that it causes it. Although this explanation is also sound, it shows the preference for it over "then you praise [Him] when you have settled." Whoever permits the use of a homonym in both its meanings may permit here that "remembrance" means both mental and verbal remembrance. But that, as you see, is far-fetched.

Since that blessing includes a marvellous matter, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and say: Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us﴾. That is, and say: Glory be to Him who made it tame and submissive to us, marvelling at that. The demonstrative here is not for belittling, but to depict the state. It contains further affirmation of the meaning of wonder. And although the statement is informative, as you heard earlier, it carries the sense of a request.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Mijlaz, who said: al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both and honour their faces, saw a man who had mounted a beast and said: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us." He said: "Were you commanded with that?" The man said: "Then how should I say it?" He said: "Say: Praise be to Allah who guided us to Islam. Praise be to Allah who bestowed on us Muhammad (ﷺ). Praise be to Allah who placed me among the best nation brought forth for mankind. Then say: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾ up to ﴿capable of it﴾." This suggests that the intended blessing is not the blessing of subjection (of the beast).

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab that he explained it as the blessing of Islam.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, and a group narrated from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, that when a mount was brought to him, and he placed his foot in the stirrup, he said: "In the name of Allah." When he settled on its back he said: "Praise be to Allah," three times, and "Allah is greatest," three times, then: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we were not capable of it, and indeed to our Lord we shall return. Glory be to You, there is no god but You; I have wronged myself, so forgive me my sins, for none forgives sins but You." Then he laughed. He was asked: "Why did you laugh, Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) do as I did, then he laughed. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, why did you laugh?' He said: 'The Lord marvels at His servant when he says: My Lord, forgive me. And He says: My servant knows that none forgives sins but Me.'"

In a hadith narrated by Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, and al-Darimi, from Ibn 'Umar: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he settled on his camel setting out on a journey, praised Allah, glorified Him, and said 'Allah is greatest' three times, then said: 'Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we were not capable of it, and indeed to our Lord we shall return.'"

In a hadith narrated by Ahmad and others from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "There is no camel but that on its hump is a devil. So mention the name of Allah when you ride it, as He commanded you."

The apparent meaning of the sublime wording is that the remembrance of the blessing and the saying mentioned are not restricted to riding livestock, but include them and the ship (*al-fulk*). Some have stated that when you board a ship you say: ﴿In the name of Allah be its course and its anchoring; indeed my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (Hud 11:41), and when you disembark you say: "O Allah, cause us to alight at a blessed place, and You are the best of those who cause to alight."

﴿And we were not capable of it﴾, that is, not able to control it. Qutrub recited for 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Indeed the tribes know that 'Aqil, for us, in calamities, are those who subdue."

This is from *aqrana al-shay'* (to be able to master something), when one is able to manage it. Ibn Harma said:

"I have borne what you laid upon me, and little is it that one can bear the endurance of aversion, O Da'd, and of abandonment."

The literal sense of *aqrana-hu* is to find him (or it) a companion (*qarina*), and that which is tied to it, because a strong thing cannot be a companion to a weak one. Do you not see how they say of the weak: "Do not tie the strong mare to it"? The *qarn* is the rope with which something is tied. The poet said:

"The son of the female camel in its second year, when he is bound in a rope, cannot withstand the assault of the mature stallion camels."

The sum of the meaning is that we have no strength by which we could control the beast and the ship; rather Allah, Exalted, is the One who subjected that and controlled it for us.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sulayman ibn Yasar that a group of people were on a journey, and whenever they mounted they would say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we were not capable of it." Among them was a man who had a female camel that was difficult to handle, and he said: "As for me, I am able to control this one." She reared up with him, threw him, and his neck was broken.

It has also been read as *muqarranina* with the *ra'* doubled, both with a fatha and with a kasra, and both have the same meaning as the unstressed form.

And indeed, to our Lord we are surely returning (﴿وإنّا إلى رَبِّنا لَمُنْقَلِبُونَ﴾). That is, we are returning. In this there is an indication that it is the right of the rider to reflect upon the journey he is undertaking and to call to mind the greater journey, which is the return (al-inqilab) to God Most High. He should then order his affairs during that journey upon this awareness, and not do anything that contradicts it. Of necessity, his riding should be for a lawful purpose. In it there is also an allusion to the fact that riding is a peril (makhatarah), so one should not be heedless in it of remembering the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 15:

﴿And they have made for Him, from among His servants, a portion.﴾ This is connected to His words, ﴿And if you ask them﴾ and so on to the end. It is therefore a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) qualifying the subject of (la-yaqūlunna), with or without the particle qad. The purpose is to show that they are contradictory and obstinate, since they acknowledged that He, glorified and exalted, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and then they ascribed to Him, glory be to Him, attributes of created beings and things that contradict His being the Creator of both. So they made for Him, glory be to Him, a portion, and said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Exalted is He far above that with a great exaltation. He expressed the offspring as a "portion" because it is a piece (ḍaḍʿa) of the one from whom it is born, as it is said: "Our children are our livers." This also indicates the extreme impossibility of this for the One Real God, to whom no division is attributed, whether in reality, by supposition, externally or mentally, exalted is His majesty and high is His station. And to emphasise the matter of contradiction, He did not suffice with His words ﴿a portion﴾. It was also said that ﴿from among His servants﴾ is added because, according to what they admit, it follows for them that whatever is in the heavens and the earth is His creation and His servant, glory be to Him, since it is originated after them and necessarily in need of them.

It was also said: al-juz' (the portion) is a term for females. It is said: "The woman bore (ajza'at) when she gave birth to a female." He cited the poet's verse:

If a free woman bore a female one day, there is no wonder; a free woman sometimes bears a male.

And his verse:

I gave her in marriage among the daughters of al-Aws, one who bears females, in whose fangs is a rattling like the supple spear-shrub.

Al-Zamakhshari regarded this as one of the innovations in interpretations (bida' al-tafasir). He stated that the claim that al-juz' in the Arabic language is a term for females is a lie against them, a newly invented and fabricated usage, and that the two verses are forged. Al-Zajjaj said of the first verse: "I do not know whether it is ancient or forged."

Some scholars justified it by saying that Hawwa' was created from a portion (juz') of Adam, peace be upon him, so the term was borrowed for all females.

Abu Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, read (juzu'an) with two dammas. Then, although the discourse is directed to the stated supposition, it implies their disbelief through likening the Creator to bodies and their disparagement of Him, exalted is He, since they ascribed to Him, glory be to Him, the lowest of the two kinds. Indeed, affirming this requires possibility, which indicates origination, so He would not be a god, a maker, or a creator, exalted is He above what they say, and glory be to Him above what they describe. The discourse is not intended to enumerate ingratitude, as some have said. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, man is ever ungrateful, manifest﴾, do not require this, for the intended meaning is hyperbole in ingratitude toward blessings, and this, in denying the Maker, is more intense than the hyperbole in their disbelief in Him, as has been indicated. (Mubin) is from abana, the intransitive form, meaning: clearly ungrateful. It is also permitted that it be from the transitive form, meaning: one who openly displays his ingratitude.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 16:

﴿Am itta-khadha mimma yakhluqu banat﴾ ("Or has He taken daughters from among what He creates?")

﴿Am﴾ is a disconnecting particle (muqatta'ah), and what it carries of meaning is "bal" (rather), for transition, while the hamzah is for denial and for expressing wonder at their state. His words, exalted is He, ﴿wa-asfakum bil-banin﴾ ("and has chosen for you sons"), are either a conjunction (ʿatf) on "itta-khadha" (took), falling under the ruling of denial and wonder, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, with "qad" implied or not implied. The turn to addressing them (iltifat ila khitabihim) is to intensify the denial, meaning: rather, He, glory be to Him, has taken for Himself from His creation the basest of the two kinds, and has chosen for you the better of the two. The sense is: suppose that attributing the taking of offspring to Him, glory be to Him, were permissible for argument's sake, do you not perceive the absurdity you have committed in the division, and the ugliness of what you claim, that He, glory be to Him, preferred you over Himself by the better and higher of the two parts, and left for Him, exalted is His station, the worse and lower of them? You are then in utmost ignorance and foolishness. The indefiniteness of "banat" (daughters) and the definiteness of "al-banin" (the sons) is due to the indication of the lowliness and the grandeur considered in each of them.

The saying of Him, exalted is He: ﴿When one of them is given the good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾. It was said that it is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause), and al-ʿAllāma al-Thānī chose this view, on the meaning that they attributed to Him, exalted is He, what they mentioned of their own condition, namely that when one of them is given good news of it, he is distressed. It was also said that it is a *istiʾnāf* (resumptive clause) confirming what precedes it, and its being conjoined to what precedes it was permitted, but that is not the right view. The *iltifāt* (shift of address) is to indicate that mentioning their ugly qualities calls for turning away from them and relating them to others in wonder. The nominal clause is in the position of the *ḥāl*, meaning: when one of them is informed of the kind of thing he has made a likeness for the Most Merciful, exalted is His majesty, which is the kind of females, because a child must be of the same kind as and similar to its parent, his face becomes utterly black because of the evil of what he has been given good news of, while he is full of anguish and sorrow.

It is related from some of the Arabs that his wife gave birth to a female, so he deserted the room in which the woman was, and she said:

What is wrong with Abu Hamza that he does not come to us,
He stays in the room that is next to us,
Angry that we do not bear sons,
And we have no say in our affair, of what we wish,
But we take what is given to us.

It was also read as *musawaddun* with a nominative ending, and as *miswādd* in the intensive form from *iswādda*, like *iḥmārra*, with the nominative as well, on the basis that in *ẓalla* there is a pronoun referring to the one given good news, and "his face is *musawaddun* or *miswādd*" is a clause occupying the position of the predicate, and the meaning is: the one given good news became black-faced. It was also said: the hidden pronoun in *ẓalla* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), and the clause is its predicate. It was also said: the verb is complete (*tāmm*), and the clause is a circumstantial clause, and the face is as previously mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who is brought up among ornaments﴾ is a repetition of the denunciation, and (man) is in the accusative position by an implied verb conjoined to (jaʿalū, "they made"). There is also an implied object here, i.e., "Did they attribute to Him, exalted is He, that it is among His affairs that one should be raised in adornment," and these are the daughters, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi said. Therefore the hamza (interrogative particle) is for denouncing the actual occurrence and deeming it abhorrent.

It has also been permitted that (man) be in the accusative by an implied verb conjoined to (ittakhadha, "He took"). In that case the hamza is for denying the occurrence and deeming it unlikely. Its insertion between the two conjoined elements serves to recall the denunciation contained in the disjunctive am (ʿamm, "or"). The conjunction is for difference in designation: i.e., "or did He, glory be to Him, take a child from this blameworthy attribute?" ﴿And he﴾, along with what has been mentioned of deficiency, ﴿in contention﴾, i.e., in disputation, from which almost no person is free ordinarily, ﴿is not clear﴾, i.e., not able to establish his claim and present his proof, because of the deficiency of his intellect and weakness of his judgment. The prepositional phrase is connected to "clear" (mubin). The attachment of (ghayr, "not") does not prevent what follows it from governing, because it carries the meaning of negation, so there is no need to make it depend on an implied element.

It has also been permitted that (man) be the subject of an omitted predicate, i.e., "Is one whose state is such-and-such, a child of His, mighty and majestic?" Some have made its predicate: "they made him a child for God, glory be to Him," or "He took him, exalted is He, as a child." It is reported from Ibn Zayd that the intended referent of "one who is raised in ornaments" is the idols. He said: They used to make many of them from gold and silver and place ornaments upon many of them. It has been objected that this view is weakened by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he in contention is not clear﴾, unless "not clear" is taken to mean the negation of contention, i.e., there is no contention from them, so "clarity" here is like the saying of the poet:

"Upon 'no love,' by whose beacon one is not guided"

In my view, this opinion is distant in itself, and the discourse, meaning His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Or has He taken﴾ up to here, comes to add further denunciation regarding their being a people whose custom is contradiction and throwing out speech without knowledge. The use of the disjunctive am and what it implies of turning away indicates that the main purpose of the discourse is to establish their ignorance and contradictoriness, not to establish their disbelief, though disbelief is understood from it, as you have heard and will hear, God willing.

Al-Jahdari, in one narration, read (yunshaʾu) with the passive voice and light form. Al-Hasan, also in one narration, read (yunashaʾu) on the pattern of yufaʿalu in the passive voice. The verbal noun of al-munashaʾa has the meaning of al-inshaʾ, like al-mughalat having the meaning of al-ighlaʾ. The majority read (yanshaʾu) in the active voice. The verse clearly indicates that growing up in adornment and softness is among the defects and blameworthy traits, and that it is among the attributes of women. So a man must avoid that, disdain it, keep himself above it, and live as ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Be rough in clothing, be rough in food, and be like the people of the desert (tamaʿaddadu)." And if he wishes to adorn himself, let him adorn his inner self with the garment of piety.

[72]

And His saying, ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾: that is, they named them and said that they are females. Al-Zajjaj said: "Making (al-ja'l) in such a usage carries the sense of saying and judging something about a thing. You say, 'I made Zayd the most knowledgeable of people,' meaning: I described him with that and judged him to be so." Abu Hayyan preferred that the meaning is: they made them females in their belief. This is an objection that comes to establish their contradiction as well, and their claim to something they have no knowledge of. This supports making it the main point of the speech in relation to what came just before, for they feminized them in this belief without basing it on any knowledge. So He guided to the fact that what they hold concerning the ascription of offspring is like what they hold concerning the feminization of the angels, peace be upon them, in that both are frivolity and ignorance. Both were disbelief at the outset. Yes, in reality both are disbelief. As for the first, it is evident. As for the second, it is because it belittles His messengers, glory be to Him, I mean the angels, and makes them the most deficient of servants in judgement and the basest of kinds, while they are the honoured servants, free of maleness and femaleness. For these are accidents of the living, nourished creature that requires the preservation of its species, since the wisdom of Allah the Exalted does not require the preservation of its individual. This is not a conjunction with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾, for, as you know, that clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿they will surely say﴾, and it is not fitting, outwardly, to say [that it is conjoined].

﴿They will surely say: The Mighty, the All-Knowing, created them﴾, while they have made the angels females. It was read as (ʿUbayd), the plural of ʿabd, and likewise (ʿIbād). It was also said that ʿIbād is the plural of ʿābid, like ṣāʾim and ṣiyām, and qāʾim and qiyām. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab read it, and al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Qatadah, Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Aʿraj, the two sons [of Kathir and ʿAmr], and Nafiʿ read (ʿinda al-Raḥmān) [with ʿinda as an adverb of place]. This reading is more indicative of the elevation of rank and nearness of station. The speech here is taken as a metaphor (istiʿārah) according to the well-known view, because locational nearness (ʿindiyyah makāniyyah) is impossible with respect to Him, glory be to Him. Ubayy read ʿAbd al-Raḥmān with a bāʾ, singular of ʿIbād, and the meaning in the plural is by intending the genus.

Al-Aʿmash read (ʿIbāda) with the plural and the accusative. Ibn Khalawayh related it and said: it is so in the codex of Ibn Masʿud. Abu Hayyan construed the accusative as implying a verb, meaning: those who were created are the servants of the Most Merciful. Zayd ibn ʿAli read (uluthan) with two ḍammahs, like kutub, as a plural of inathan [i.e., a plural of the plural]. In all readings, the restriction (ḥaṣr), if it is taken as relative (idāfī), does not complete the argument it is used for, namely the superiority of the angel over the human.

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ That is: were they present at Allah the Exalted's creating them, so that they witnessed them as females and could judge them to be female? For that is something known by observation. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ In it is a rebuke of them and a mockery of them. The verse did not address the negation of transmitted proofs, because in this kind of inquiry those proofs are founded upon the affirmation of prophethood, and these are the disbelievers who do not affirm it. Nor did it address the negation of rational proofs, because their non-existence is evident. The stated negation is more apparent in mockery, so understand.

Nafiʿ read (a-ush-hadū) with a hamzah entering upon (ushhida), the quadriliteral in the passive. In one transmission he eased this hamzah, making it between a hamzah and a wāw, and this is a transmission from Abu ʿAmr. It was also related from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, and from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. In another transmission he eased it and inserted an alif between it and the first, out of dislike for two hamzahs coming together. This is attributed to a group. Relying on easing alone is more preferable.

Al-Zuhri and others read (ushhidū) without the interrogative, in the passive, quadriliteral. It was said that the meaning is interrogative, like the line of poetry:

"They said, 'Do you love her?' I said, 'Vehemently.'"

This is the apparent meaning. It was also said that it is declarative, and the clause is a qualifier of (uluthan) [females]. Although they did not witness their creation, by their audacity in this they were placed in the position of one who was made to witness. Or the intended meaning is that they applied the term "females" to them, referring to the well-known females who were witnessed in their creation, not to another kind of females. There is no concealing the artifice in both of these interpretations.

﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾ in the register of their deeds, ﴿the testimony they gave concerning the angels, peace be upon them.﴾ It was also said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked them: "What makes you know that they are females?" They said: "We heard that from our fathers, and we bear witness that they did not lie." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ about it on the Day of Resurrection. The speech is a threat to them of punishment and recompense for that, and the sīn is for emphasis. It was also said that it is permissible to take it upon its apparent meaning of the future, and that this indicates a deferral of recording evil deeds in hope of repentance and return, as was reported in the hadith: "The recorder of good deeds is trustworthy over the recorder of evil deeds. When he wants to write it down, he is told: 'Hold back.' He holds back for seven hours. If he seeks forgiveness and repents, he does not write it down." Since this is the nature of recording, it was joined with the sīn. That they are disbelievers who persist in disbelief does not preclude this.

Al-Zuhri read (sayuktabu), with the yāʾ of the third person and the passive. Al-Hasan read like the majority, except that he read (shahādātihim), in the plural. This is their saying that Allah, glory be to Him, has a portion, that He has daughters, and that they are the angels. It was also said that what is meant is what was intended by the singular and the plural, in terms of repetition.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, al-Jahdari, and al-Aʿraj read (sanaktubu), with the nūn, in the active, (shahādatahum), in the accusative and singular.

A group read (sayaktubu), with the yāʾ of the third person, in the active, and (shahādatahum) in the singular and accusative. That is: Allah the Exalted will record their testimony.

It was read (yusāʾalūna), from the form of mufāʿalah, for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 20:

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ It is coordinated with His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿And they made the angels﴾ etc., indicating that it is of the same kind as their claim that the angels are female, in that they said it without knowledge. Their intention by this statement, according to what some of the eminent scholars have said, is to argue from the negation of God Most High's will (regarding) the abandonment of worship of the angels, peace be upon them, to the impermissibility of forbidding it or to its goodness. It is as though they said: God Most High did not will that we abandon worshipping the angels; had He, glory be to Him, willed that, it would have been realised. Rather, He, exalted is His majesty, willed worship, since it is what has come to be, so it must be commanded, or good, and it is impossible for it to be forbidden or ugly. This is a false argument, because will does not entail command or goodness, since it is the preponderance of some possibilities over others, whether good or ugly. Therefore, by His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, they were refuted regarding the statement in the way they intended it. Its upshot returns to an indication of their assumption that will necessitates that the command conform to it, or the goodness of what it is attached to, ﴿of knowledge﴾ that rests on any authority.

﴿They do not but guess﴾, i.e., they lie, as one of many has explained it, and "kharṣ" (conjecture, guessing) is used for estimation, which is common.

Rather, it was said that it is the original meaning; and in every case it is a saying based on conjecture and speculation,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this (Qur'an), so that they are holding fast to it?﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from negating that they have knowledge of this by way of reason, to nullifying that they have any support (sanad) from the side of transmission (naql). So "am" (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), not connective (muttasilah) and equivalent to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did they witness...?﴾ as has been said, due to its remoteness. The pronoun in (qablihi) refers to the Qur'an, as it is known from the context, or to the Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace. The sin in (mustamsikun) is for emphasis (ta'kid), not for demand (talab). That is: rather, We have given them a Book before the Qur'an, or before the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, speaking to the soundness of what they claim, so they are holding fast to that Book and relying upon it,

[p. 74]

The words of Him, Majestic and Exalted, ﴿Nay, they say: "We found our fathers following a religion, and we are guided by their footsteps"﴾ are a refutation of any proof they might have for this, in the sense that they have no proof at all for it, neither rational nor transmitted. They only inclined to it by imitating their fathers, who were ignorant like them. The word *ummah* (religion, creed, and path that is followed, as a journey is undertaken to a great man who is sought in important matters) is used in the sense of religion and path. One says, "So-and-so has no *ummah*," meaning he has no religion or creed. The poet said:

"Can one who has a faith be equal to an ingrate?"

Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"We were upon the religion of our fathers,
and the latter follows the first."

Al-Jubba'i said: *ummah* means "community," and the intended meaning is that "we found our fathers in agreement upon this." The majority hold the first meaning, and it is the one relied upon. It is also said *immah* with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Jahdari recited it this way.

Ibn Ayyash recited *ummatin* with a *fatha* on the *hamza*. Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*): that is, "with an intention and a state." As for ﴿upon their footsteps are guided﴾, it is said that the two are predicates of *inna*. It is also said that ﴿upon their footsteps﴾ is a complement of ﴿guided﴾, and ﴿guided﴾ is the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari took this verse as evidence that God did not will disbelief from the disbeliever, and that He, glorified be He, willed only faith. The People of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the orthodox majority), who hold that all that is decreed occurs by the will of God Most High, declared him an unbeliever. He explained this by saying that when the disbelievers claimed that God had willed their disbelief, saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾, etc., meaning: if the Majestic One had willed that we abandon worshipping idols, we would have abandoned it, God Most High rejected this claim against them and nullified their belief by His words, glorified be He: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, etc. Thus the consequence is the actual opposite of what they claimed, which is exactly what he (al-Zamakhshari) held. The sentence is coordinated with the words of God Most High, ﴿and they have made of His servants a part of Him﴾, or with "they have made the angels" etc. Thus what it contains would be another disbelief, and the disbelief of those who say that everything is by His will is necessarily implied. From what you have heard, its refutation is known.

It is also said, in refuting this: it is possible that this refers to the basic claim, which is the making of the angels, peace be upon them, daughters of God, glorified and exalted be He far above that, rather than what they intended by their words "if He had willed" etc. What is mentioned after the basic claim is part of its completion, for it recounts their deluded doubt, since worship of the angels, even if by His will, does not negate that it is among the most evil of the abominations forbidden. This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Some eminent scholars said: their disbelief in this was because they said it in mockery. Al-Zamakhshari rejected this, saying: the context does not indicate that they said it mockingly; He, Exalted be He, has related about them, in a manner of reproach and testimony to their disbelief, that they made for Him a part, that He took daughters and chose sons for Himself, that they made the honored angels females, that they worshipped them, and that they said, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." So if they were speaking these words in a way of mockery, then the speaking of the reported statements before this reported statement, which is faith in his view, would be a praise for them, because these are words of disbelief which they uttered in mockery. So what remains is that they were serious. All of them share in being words of disbelief. If they make only the last one said in mockery, without what precedes it, then they are merely distorting the Book of God. And if this were a word of truth which they uttered in mockery, then His words, ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, etc., would have no meaning, because the obligation regarding one who speaks the truth in mockery is that his mockery be rebuked, not that he be called a liar.

It is not hidden that his refutation, that the context does not indicate this, is correct. As for what was mentioned about God's relating and about distortion, it is not so, because He, Exalted be He, did not first relate a statement about them; rather He attributed to them a belief which contains a statement or an action, and He clarified that they are frivolous in that conviction just as they are frivolous in this statement. So His words, "If they spoke," etc., have no bearing on what preceded, and there is no distortion whatsoever in this respect. Likewise his statement, "it would have no meaning for His words, ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾," etc., is rejected, because mockery is a branch of ignorance, as is shown by the words of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿I seek refuge in God lest I be among the ignorant﴾, and this was mentioned in *al-Baqara*. As for lying, it refers to its content, and what is meant by it is as you have heard. So whoever says "There is no god but God" in mockery is a liar regarding what it entails, that it is a report of affirming plurality, because it is a report of tawhid (the oneness of God). So understand.

Also in it: that their words, ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed﴾, etc., are understood as disbelief in several respects.

The first is that it is an excuse for their worship of the angels, peace be upon them, which is disbelief, and an argument that if it is by His will, Exalted be He, it is not reprehensible.

The second is that disbelief and faith are by affirming or denying what is necessarily known to be established, whether self-evidently or by inference, related to the origin and the return, and not by the performance of an act in accordance with the will or its absence.

The third is that they repelled the Messenger's statement, by calling them to the worship of Him, Exalted be He, and forbidding them to worship other than Him, with this saying. Then they are bound by the course of this statement, because if everything is attributed to the will of God Most High, then He willed the sending of the messengers, willed their call to the servants, willed their denial, and willed, Exalted be He, that they enter the Fire. So denial and repulsion after this statement is evidence that they said it not out of belief but out of recklessness. To this points His words in a similar context: ﴿Say: "To God belongs the conclusive proof. Had He willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ And in it: they weaken the Creator by asserting a conflict between His will and the opposite of what He commanded, so that it follows that He wills only what He has commanded, and does not forbid what He does not will, glorified be He. This is a weakening in two respects: removing some of what is decreed from being its locus, and narrowing the locus of His command and prohibition. This is exactly the doctrine of their brethren, the Qadariyya (a school that affirms human free will against divine decree). For this reason, their statement "And they said: if the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them" was made the principal point of the discourse, and it was not said: "they worshipped the angels and said: 'If He had willed.'" Its counterpart in the sense that it was only brought to repel what is known necessarily is His statement, Exalted be He, about them: ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾. So the repulsion is a disbelief, and the weakening is a disbelief upon a disbelief.

His words, Exalted be He, ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, may refer to all that preceded from His words ﴿and they have made of His servants a part of Him﴾ up to this point, and may refer to the last. It has been established that they said it without knowledge, and this is the more apparent because of proximity, and because each is followed by an independent denial. Its correspondence with what is in *al-An'am* and His words, glorified be He: ﴿They only guess﴾, following this denial implied by it, relates to the conclusion of the purpose of this conditional statement. It was already said that it is against them and not for them, and it hinted at a part of it in *Surat al-An'am*. Or it refers to the judgment of the impossibility of separation, together with the judge's permission of separation while he judges, for that indicates the falsity of his judgment, even if that judgment is in itself true and correct, which it is right to know, as you say, "Zayd is standing, certainly" or "definitely," while you have the possibility of its opposite.

This is not a return to the doctrine of those who make truth consist in its correspondence to belief. So understand. Moreover, since it was an excuse for what passed, it is valid that the denial refers to its not being fit to be an excuse, that is: they are lying in the claim that the will requires the conformity of the command to it. This is what the Imam, the Allama, and al-Qadi preferred, though the apparent meaning is what we have already put forward.

The placement of "guessing" as clarification or as a new sentence after His words, ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, and His words, ﴿They only follow conjecture﴾ in *Surat al-An'am*, is evidence of what we have indicated. It has become clear to the one seeking guidance that the verse is fit as a proof for the People of the Sunna, not for the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school which asserts human agency and divine justice).

He said regarding the verse in *Surat al-An'am*: their statement is either for the claim of legitimacy, rejecting the messengers, or for conceding that they are upon falsehood, offering the excuse that they are compelled. The first is false, because the will is related to their act, whether legitimate or otherwise. So what God, Exalted be He, willed to occur from them as legitimate occurred as such, and what God, Exalted be He, willed to occur not as such occurred not as such.

There is no doubt that whoever imagines that the act being by the will of God Most High contradicts the coming of the messengers, peace be upon them, in contrast to what the performer is upon of disbelief and error, has denied the entire denial, and he is lying in the conclusion of the purpose of this conditional statement. The apparent meaning of the verse is directed to this meaning. The second, despite what it contains of achieving the purpose, which is the acknowledgment of nullity, is also false, because there is no compulsion, since the will is related to their associating by their own choice, and the knowledge is related in the same way. So it confirms the rejection of predestination, rather than establishing it. To this points His words: ﴿Say: "To God belongs the conclusive proof."﴾ Then they are lying in this statement, because of their certainty where there is no conjecture at all, let alone knowledge. This is because it is known that knowledge of the attributes of God, glorified be He, is a branch of knowledge of His essence, Exalted be He, and faith in them is likewise. Those who argue with this are disbelievers, polytheists, and anthropomorphists (*mujassima*, those who attribute bodily form to God).

Al-Allama al-Tibi quoted something similar to the last statement from Imam al-Haramayn, may God have mercy on him, in *al-Irshad*. End.

The great scholars have extended the discussion at this point. I see that this man, may God water his resting place with the rain of His good pleasure, has churned all of that and brought out its butter. Indeed, he left no verification for those who come after him. So reflect. And God, Mighty and Majestic, is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 23:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., the matter is as has been mentioned: their inability to produce any proof whatsoever, and their clinging to the hem of imitation (taqlid, blind adherence to tradition). His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿We sent not before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said: "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that is not grammatically dependent on what precedes it) explaining that, and indicating that imitation among them is an ancient error inherited from their forefathers, and that their predecessors likewise had no sound basis to which they could look. The specification of the affluent (mutrafun) with this statement serves to signal that luxury and love of idleness diverted them from reflecting on the matter and turned them toward imitation. ﴿He said﴾ is a report of what took place between the warners and their peoples when the latter pleaded the imitation of their fathers, i.e., each warner from among those warners said to his community:

﴿Even if I brought you﴾, i.e., "Will you follow your fathers even if I brought you ﴿with a religion more guided﴾, with a religion more guided ﴿than that which you found your fathers upon﴾ of misguidance, which has no share of guidance at all? He expressed it this way only as a concession to them, following the path of fairness."

The majority of readers recited (qul, "say") as a narration of a past command that was revealed to every warner, meaning: it was said, or We said to the warner, "Say, ..." etc. Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) favoured that it is an address to our Prophet ﷺ. The apparent meaning is what preceded it, due to the words of Allah, ﴿They said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ For it is very clear that this is a narration about the earlier nations, meaning: every nation said to its warner, "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent," etc. The narration was summarized for brevity, as was established in the words of Allah, ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾.

Whoever takes it as a narration about his people, peace be upon him, by reading the plural form as giving precedence to the Prophet ﷺ over the rest of the warners, and directing their disbelief to what all of them were sent with, which is monotheism, because all of them, peace be upon them, agreed on it, as in the words of Allah, ﴿The people of ʿĀd denied the messengers﴾, is a far-fetched contrivance. Also, the apparent meaning rejects it,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 26:**

﴿And when Abraham said﴾, meaning: mention to them the time when he, upon him be peace, said ﴿to his father﴾ Azar ﴿and his people﴾, who were absorbed in *taqlid* (blind imitation of tradition), how he disassociated himself from what they were upon, by his saying:

﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. He also held fast to proof. The statement is a preface to what the people of Makkah were engaged in of obstinacy, envy, and refusal to reflect upon the signs, and that if they had imitated their forefathers, it would have been more fitting for them to imitate their father who was the most excellent and most knowledgeable, the one they boast of belonging to, namely Abraham, peace be upon him. So it is as if, after rebuking them for *taqlid*, he rebukes them for being wrong in also neglecting his choice. *Barā'* (free from) is a verbal noun like *talāq*, used as an adjective for emphasis, and therefore it applies equally to the singular and plural, and the masculine and feminine.

Al-Za'farani and al-Qawrasi, from Abu Ja'far, and Ibn al-Munadhiri, from Nafi', read (*Burā'*) with a *ḍammah* on the *bā'*, which is a singular noun like *ṭawāl* and *kurām* with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*. Al-A'mash read (*Barī'*), which is a descriptive adjective like *ṭawīl* and *karīm*. The common reading is the dialect of al-'Aliyah, and this is the dialect of Najd.

Al-A'mash also read (*Innī*) with a shaddah on the *nūn*, without the *nūn al-wiqāyah*.

﴿Except He who created me﴾: this is a continuous exception (istithna' muttasil), if we say that "ma" (in ﴿ma ta'budun﴾) is general, covering rational beings and others, and that they used to worship God Most High as well as idols. This is not the kind of association of God Most High with others, which must be avoided, because it would give the false impression of equality between Him, glorified be He, and something else. The apparent meaning of the speech shows otherwise. Alternatively, it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), based on the view that "ma" is specific to non-rational beings, that it is not appropriate to use the taghlib (the grammatical device of giving precedence to the masculine rational form) at all, and that they did not worship Him, Exalted is He. Or they did worship Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, but His worship together with association (shirk) is considered as non-existent. On both views, the position of the relative pronoun (al-ladhi) is in the accusative case.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the genitive case, as a substitute (badal) for "ma," which is governed by the preposition "min." There is a point of discussion here, because it would then become an exception from an affirmative statement (istithna' min al-muwjab), and they did not permit substitution in that case. Its justification is that it carries the sense of negation, since the meaning of ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾ is "I do not worship what you worship." It is therefore like the statement of God Most High: ﴿And God refuses except that He perfect His light﴾. However, that example is of the type called "mufarragh" (an exception with the stated item omitted), whereas this case concerns one in which the item excepted from is stated, and they do not restrict this rule to the mufarragh type, nor to specific words such as "aba" (refused) and "qalama" (rarely). Yes, Abu Hayyan insists on refusing this, holding that the sentence is affirmative and does not treat negation as a meaning.

He also permitted that "illa" be an adjective (sifah) with the meaning of "ghayr" (other than), with "ma" in ﴿ma ta'budun﴾ being an indefinite noun described by a following clause, and the sense being: "Indeed, I am free from gods that you worship, other than He who created me." This is like the statement of God Most High: ﴿Had there been in them gods except God, they would have been corrupted﴾. Treating "ma" as an indefinite described noun is based on the view that "illa" is not used as an adjective except after an indefinite noun. Likewise, treating it as having the meaning of the plural is based on the condition that the indefinite noun described by it must be so. The matter is one of scholarly disagreement. Among the grammarians, some said that "illa" may describe both definite and indefinite nouns in general, and on this view there is no need to regard "ma" as an indefinite noun meaning "gods."

Placing the relative clause ﴿fataranī﴾ (who created me) indicates that worship is due only to the Creator of the worshipper. ﴿So He will guide me﴾: He will keep me firm upon guidance. The "sin" (in sayahdini) is for emphasis, not for the future tense, because the same verb occurs in the poets' passage as "yahdini" without it, and the story is one and the same. The present tense in both places denotes continuity. It has also been said that the intended meaning of ﴿sayahdini﴾ is "to a guidance beyond that to which He had first guided me," so the "sin" retains its literal sense, and the difference lies in the narration and the narrated matter, on the basis that the story is repeated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 28:

﴿And He made it﴾ The hidden nominative pronoun refers to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), or to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The accusative pronoun refers to the word of tawhid (monotheism), namely "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh), as narrated from Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Suddi. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾, and so on. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to this statement itself, which is also a "word" (kalimah) linguistically. ﴿A word that remains among his descendants﴾, that is, among his offspring (peace be upon him), so there will always be among them someone who affirms the oneness of Allah, Exalted is He, and calls to His tawhid, Mighty and Majestic.

Ḥumayd ibn Qays read (kilmatan) with a kasrah on the kaf and a sukun on the lam, and this is a dialectal form of it. It was also read (fī ʿaqbihi) with a sukun on the qaf for lightness, and (fī ʿāqibihi), meaning "among those who come after him," that is, his successors. From this is the naming of the Prophet (ﷺ) as al-ʿĀqib, because he is the last of the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them).

﴿So that they may return﴾ This is a reason for the making: that is, He made it remain among his descendants so that whoever among them associated partners with Allah may return through the supplication of those who affirmed His oneness, or because of its remaining among them. The two pronouns refer to "ʿaqib," which carries the sense of plurality. Most scholars hold that the speech contains an elided noun, meaning "so that their polytheists may return," or the attribution is one of attributing to the part what belongs to the whole. Some interpreters explained "laʿalla" (so that/perhaps) on the basis that the expression of hope (tarajji) comes from Allah, Glorified is He, which is not valid regarding Him, Exalted is He; or that it comes from him (peace be upon him), but for the prophets it has the status of something certain. Abandoning this interpretation is permissible, as is evident; rather, it is the more apparent reading if that statement is from Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 29:**

﴿Nay, I gave these people enjoyment﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah who were contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿and their forefathers﴾, by extending to them life and blessings, ﴿until there came to them the Truth﴾, the call to monotheism (tawhid), or the Qur'an, ﴿and a clear Messenger﴾, one whose message is manifest through his dazzling miracles, or one who makes monotheism clear through the clear signs and decisive proofs. The enjoyment (tamti') here means what causes it: their delight in what they were given, and their preoccupation with it, which diverted them from thanking the Benefactor and obeying Him. The purpose (ghayah) of this is as if it were said: "They remained preoccupied until the Truth came." In reality this is also a purpose of the matter itself, because the coming of a Messenger is something that awakens from the custom of heedlessness and restrains from being absorbed in pleasures. But they reversed matters: they made what was a cause of turning back into a cause of plunging deeper. This is in the manner of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved were not going to leave off…﴾ up to His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And those given the Scripture did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾.

﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from His, may His majesty be great, saying: ﴿so that they might return﴾. It is as if it were said: "Nay, I gave enjoyment to the polytheists of Makkah and occupied them with amusements and pleasures, so they were preoccupied and did not return," or "what He hoped for, of their returning from polytheism, did not come about." In reality this is a turning away from the preamble you have heard and a beginning of the main subject, but the connection was observed in it by what is close to the clause of the turning away, namely ﴿so that they might return﴾.

In the Shihabi glosses (al-Hawashi al-Shihabiyya) it is said that it is a turning away from His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And He made it﴾ etc., i.e., they did not return, so I did not hasten the punishment upon them; rather I gave them other blessings besides the enduring word, so that they would thank their Bestower and make Him one, but they did not do so, and their rebellion only increased through their deception. Or the implied meaning is: I was not content, in guiding them, with making the word remain among them; rather I gave them enjoyment and sent a Messenger.

Qatadah and al-A'mash read (﴿Nay, You gave enjoyment﴾) with the second person (ta' of address), and Ya'qub related it from Nafi'. It is part of His own speech by way of tajrid (speaking in the voice of another within one's own address), not iltifat (shift of grammatical person), although iltifat has been said of its like as well. It is as if He, exalted be He, raised an objection against Himself in His saying: ﴿And He made it﴾ etc., not to censure His own act, glorified be He, but for the purpose of increasing the reproach of the polytheists. This is like when a benefactor says, addressing himself regarding one who has done evil: "You are the one who invited his evil by your kindness to him and your care for him." His speech thus appears in the form of one who objects against himself and rebukes himself, until it is as if he deserves that, and in this there is much reproach of the wrongdoer.

The author of al-Lawami' said: it is from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, and his intimate supplication to his Lord, may He be mighty and majestic. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): the apparent meaning is that it is from the intimate supplication of the Messenger (ﷺ), in the sense of "Say: O Lord, I gave enjoyment…" The first view is preferable, and it is the one that agrees with the well-known principle.

Al-A'mash read (﴿We gave enjoyment﴾) with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah).

﴿When the truth came to them﴾, to awaken them from the heedlessness they were in and to guide them to monotheism, ﴿they said, "This is magic, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾
