﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of great standing from the two cities?"﴾ That is, from one of the two cities, Makkah and al-Ta'if, or from their men. So "min" (مِنَ) here is either for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah) or partitive (tab'idiyyah). It is also read as (رَجْلٍ) with the letter jim sukun. ﴿Great﴾ in rank and wealth. Ibn 'Abbas said: the one from Makkah was al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, and the one from al-Ta'if was Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi. Mujahid said: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and Kinanah ibn 'Abd Yalil. Qatadah said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah was called "the basil of Quraysh" (rayhanat Quraysh), and he used to say: "If what Muhammad (ﷺ) says were true, it would have been sent down upon me, or upon Abu Mas'ud," meaning 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud, who was known by that kunyah. This is another aspect of their denial of prophethood. They first denied that the Prophet could be a human being, and then, when they were rebuked by the repetition of proofs and no conception of that denial remained with them, they came with denial from another angle, and so they dictated to Allah, glorified is He, that the Messenger be one of these two men. Their statement "this Qur'an" (هَذا القُرْآنُ) is a mention of it in a manner of contempt, because they did not make this statement in acceptance, but in denial, as if it were said: "This lie that he claims, if it were true, the one most fitting for it would be a great man from the two cities." This was from them due to their ignorance that the rank of prophethood requires only greatness of soul through being free of base vices and adorned with perfections and sacred virtues, not through being adorned with worldly ornaments.

﴿Do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ This is a rebuke that implies ignorance and expresses wonder at their presumption in dictating the sending down of the Mighty Qur'an to whomever they wish. As for "mercy" (rahmah), it may mean its literal sense, which is the apparent meaning of al-Bahr's words. Their designating whom the revelation should descend upon is treated as if it were an apportioning of it, and prophethood is included within it. It may also mean prophethood, which is more suitable to what precedes it, and most exegetes hold this view. In the attribution of "Lord" to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, there is what there is of honouring him, peace be upon him. In the attribution of "mercy" to "Lord" there is an indication that it is among the attributes of lordship.

﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood﴾, meaning the means of their livelihood.

Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, al-A'mash, and Sufyan read (maʿayishahum), in the plural, ﴿in the life of this world﴾, as an apportionment required by Our will, which is founded upon wisdoms and interests. We did not delegate its matter to them, knowing from Us their inability to manage it entirely. The unqualified term "livelihood" implies that both its lawful and unlawful aspects are from Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿And We have raised some of them above others﴾ in provision and all the other sources of subsistence, ﴿in degrees﴾, varying according to nearness and distance, as wisdom requires. So there is the weak and the strong, the rich and the poor, the servant and the served, the ruler and the ruled. ﴿So that some of them may take others in service (sukhriyyan)﴾, so that some use others for their interests, employ them in their trades, and have them work at their tasks, so that they may live together, support one another, and reach their needs. This is not for any perfection in the one who is granted abundance, nor for any deficiency in the one who is restricted. Had We left that to their own management, they would have been lost and destroyed. If they, in managing their own petty affairs and what benefits them of the base goods of this world, are in this state, on the verge of completion, then what is their opinion of themselves in managing the affair of religion? That is far more distant than the star al-ʿUyuq (a star in the sky). And from where would they have the means to investigate the matter of prophethood and to choose for it whoever is fit for it and able to bear its burden?

As for sukhriyy (in the sense you have heard), it is a relative noun derived from sukhrah, meaning subjugation and imposition of work. Al-Raghib said: sukhriyy is one who is subjugated, who is compelled to be made subservient by another's will. Some claimed that here it derives from sakhr meaning mockery, i.e., that the rich may mock the poor, but Abu Hayyan considered this unlikely. Al-Samin said that it is not suitable to the context.

Amr ibn Maymun, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Raja', and al-Walid ibn Muslim read (sikhriyyan) with a kasrah on the sin. What is meant by it is also what we have mentioned. In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We have apportioned﴾, and so on, there is that which discourages eager pursuit of the pursuit of this world and helps one to rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to devote oneself to Him, glorious is His majesty:

So reflect: "We have apportioned among them," and you will find it true; and with truth it was sent down.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾, that is, prophethood and what follows from it of the happiness of both abodes. It has been said: it is guidance and faith. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is Paradise. ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of the base and lowly goods of this world. So the great one is the one who is granted that mercy rather than that base, perishable plunder.

Page 79

﴿Had it not been that mankind would be one community, We would have given to those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and stairways upon which they would ascend﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh point) that clarifies the worthlessness of the goods of this world and the lowliness of their value in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning is that the insignificance of this worldly matter is such that, were it not for the aversion to people gathering together upon disbelief and unanimously adopting it, We would have given such goods to whoever is the worst of creation and the lowest in station, in the most complete manner. Thus, the aversion to collective disbelief is what prevents granting every disbeliever enjoyment and expanding provision for him, not that the obstacle is that worldly goods have value in Our sight. The aforementioned aversion is the wisdom behind withholding comfort from every disbeliever and expanding provision upon him, so there is no omitted element in its estimation. This is not based on the obligation to safeguard the public interest (maslahah) or on Allah willing faith from creation, so as to be a form of Mu'tazilite doctrine (i'tizal) as some have supposed. It seems that the reason why expanding provision on the disbelievers would be a cause of people gathering upon disbelief is the excessive love of people for this world: when they see that, they disbelieve in order to obtain it. This is in the sense that Allah, exalted is His majesty, knew that had He done so, the people's love of this world would then have called them to disbelief. Therefore, it should not be said that many people today would attain complete wealth if they disbelieved, yet they do not disbelieve, even if they were compelled to it by killing. And it should not be said that what is meant by the single matter that their being one community requires is that they gather upon one matter, namely disbelief, by the indication of the answer (the apodosis of the conditional clause),

Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, commentary on surah 43, verse 34:

﴿And for their houses﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive substitution, a substitute that includes its antecedent in meaning) of his words, exalted is He: ﴿for those who disbelieve﴾. The *lam* in both phrases indicates *ikhtisas* (specification or attribution). Alternatively, both are connected to the verb, not as a substitution. The *lam* in ﴿for those who﴾ is connected to the verb, because the verb is transitive through the *lam*, so it functions as the direct object. The *lam* in ﴿for their houses﴾ indicates purpose (*ta'lil*), so it functions as the object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). It is permissible that the first is for ownership (*milk*) and the second for specification, as in your saying: "I gave the rope to Zayd for his animal." This is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya. If the two *lam*s differ, substitution in meaning is not permissible, because the requirement of repeating the governing word in the substitute is unity of meaning. This is the view of Abu Hayyan. Al-Khafaji said: there is no obstacle to the whole being substituted for the whole without considering a repetition.

The word (سُقُفًا) is the plural of (سَقْف), like (رُهُنٌ), the plural of (رَهْن). It is related from al-Farra' that it is the plural of (سَقِيفَة), like (سُفُنٌ), the plural of (سَفِينَة). (المَعارِجُ) is the plural of (مَعْرِج), and it is coordinated with (سُقُفًا), meaning: and We would have made for them ascents upon which they rise to the roofs and upper floors. It seems that the intended meaning is ascents of silver, based on the view that coordination shows sharing of the qualifier, even if it comes earlier. Abu Hayyan said: this is not necessarily so.

Abu Raja' read (سُقْفًا) with a *damma* on the *sin* and a sukun on the *qaf* as a lightening. In al-Bahr, this is the dialect of Tamim.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (سَقْفًا) with a *fatha* on the *sin* and a sukun, in the singular, because it is a noun of genus (*ism jins*) that applies to one and to more, and this is what is meant by the context of "houses." It was also read with a *fatha* on the *sin* and the *qaf*, and this is a dialect for (سَقْف). This is not the moving of a silent letter, because there is no basis for that.

It was read (سُقُوفًا), which is the plural of (سَقْف), like (فُلُوسٌ), the plural of (فَلْس). Talha read (مَعارِيجَ), the plural of (مِعْراج). ﴿And for their houses﴾ means: and We would have made for their houses. The repetition of mention of their houses is for added emphasis, and because it begins a new verse. ﴿Doors and couches﴾ means of silver, as you have heard. It was read (سَرَرًا) with a *fatha* on the *sin* and the *ra*, a dialect of Banu Tamim and some of Kalb. This is in the plural of the doubled form of *fa'il* when it is a noun, by agreement, and when it is an adjective, as in (ثَوْبٌ جَدِيدٌ) and (ثِيابٌ جُدُدٌ), by difference among the grammarians. ﴿Upon them﴾ means: upon the couches, reclining (يَتَّكِؤُنَ), as is the way of kings, to whom nothing matters.

[p. 80]

﴿وَزُخْرُفًا﴾ Al-Hasan said: that is, decorations and embellishments. Ibn Zayd said: *al-zukhruf* is the furnishings of the house and its movable goods. He takes it as coordinated (*ʿatf*) with *suqufan* (roofs). Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Shaʿbi, al-Suddi, and al-Hasan again in one narration, said: *al-zukhruf* is gold. Most lexicographers mentioned both of these meanings for it, along with adornment in general. It was said: the apparent meaning is that the word is literal in both senses. It was also said: it is literal in the sense of adornment, and because the perfection of adornment is through gold, it is also used for gold. Al-Raghib's statement points to this. He said: *al-zukhruf* is adornment that is embellished, and from this gold is called *zukhruf*. In *al-Bahr* it is said that a hadith states: "Beware of red, for it is among the most beloved adornments to Satan." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: beauty is red, and desires follow it. One of the poets of the Maghrib said:

"You dyed your armour with the blood of their slain, when you saw beauty clothed in red."

On this view, it is coordinated (*ʿatf*) with the grammatical position (*mahall*) of ﴿مِن فِضَّةٍ﴾ (of silver), as if the original were "roofs of silver and ornament," meaning some of them of silver and some of them of gold. It was put in the accusative as coordination with the position. It is also permitted to coordinate it with *suqufan* (roofs).

﴿وَإِنْ كُلُّ ذَلِكَ لَمَّا مَتَاعُ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا﴾ (And all that is but the enjoyment of the life of this world). That is: all that has been mentioned of the houses described with the detailed attributes is only something enjoyed in the life of this world. Similar in meaning is the reading that was recited: "وَمَا كُلُّ ذَلِكَ إِلَّا مَتَاعُ الدُّنْيَا" (And all that is nothing but the enjoyment of the world).

The majority read *lamma* (لَمَّا) with a fatha on the lam and a light pronunciation. Here *in* (إنْ) is the light form (*mukhaffafah*) of the heavy *inna*, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (*lam al-fariqah*) that separates the light form from the negation particle. *Ma* is either extra (*zaidah*) or a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), with the sense of *lamma huwa matāʿun* (what is an enjoyment). This is like the Almighty's words ﴿تَمَامًا عَلَى الَّذِي أَحْسَنَ﴾ (as a completion [of favour] upon the one who did good), in the reading of those who put a *damma* on the nun.

Abu Haywah and Raja' (and in *al-Tahrir*, Abu Hayah) read *limā* (لِمَا) with a kasra on the lam and a light pronunciation. Here *in* is the light form, the lam is a preposition (*harf jarr*), and *ma* is a relative pronoun in the position of a preposition's object. The prepositional phrase is in the position of the predicate of *kull* (all). The beginning of the relative clause is omitted, as you heard just now.

The usual construction in such a case is to bring the distinguishing lam, so one would say *lalamma matāʿun* (indeed it is an enjoyment). But it was dropped because the intention of affirmation is clear, as in the poet's words:

"I am the son of those who refuse oppression, of the family of Malik, and though Malik's people were noble of origin."

Indeed, in the verse it is not permissible to insert the lam, as is not hidden from the grammarian.

﴿وَالْآخِرَةُ﴾ (And the Hereafter), that is, with what it contains of the various kinds of bliss which the scope of expression cannot encompass, ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ (is with your Lord for the righteous), specifically for them. By "the righteous" are meant those who guard against polytheism. Others said: those who guard against that and against sins.

The verse contains an indication of discouraging attachment to this world and its adornments, and of encouraging piety. Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn Majah related from Sahl ibn Saʿd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If this world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it."

From ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face): "The world is more worthless than the foreleg of a dead pig upon which a dog urinated in the hand of a leper."

Some scholars also used the Almighty's words ﴿لِبُيُوتِهِمْ سُقُفًا﴾ (roofs for their houses) as evidence that the roof belongs to the owner of the lower house, not to the owner of the upper floor, because it is attributed to the house.

﴿Wa-man ya'shu﴾ (And whoever turns a blind eye to), that is, feigns blindness and turns away, ﴿'an dhikri al-Rahman﴾ (from the remembrance of the Most Merciful). The remembrance here is the Qur'an. Its attribution to al-Rahman indicates that it was sent down as a mercy to the worlds. It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun (masdar) in the genitive of the object, meaning: whoever is blind to remembering al-Rahman. And it is permitted that it be a verbal noun in the genitive of the subject, meaning: from al-Rahman's reminding His servants, glory be to Him. Yahya ibn Sallam al-Basri recited (ya'sha) with a fatha on the shin, like (yarda), meaning (ya'ma), a form said of one who is afflicted in his sight. It is said: 'ashiya (like radiya) when an affliction has occurred in his sight, and 'asha (like ghaza) when he looks with the gaze of one who has night blindness (ashan) due to some accident. Al-Hutay'ah said:

"Whenever you come to him, you squint toward the light of his fire; you will find the best fire there, and the best kindler."

That is, you look at it with the gaze of one with night blindness, because of the weakness that the great size of the fuel and the wide extent of the light cause to your sight. Had it not been so, the word "ghayah" (until/to the extent) would have no fitting place. Clearer in meaning is the saying of Hatim:

"I squint when my neighbour appears, until the curtain conceals my neighbour."

This is because it is restricted by a time and is accompanied by a limit, whereas the blindness that is innate does not cease. Some of them said: I have not seen anyone permit "'ashawtu 'anhu" (I turned a blind eye to him) in the sense of "a'radta" (you turned away). Rather it is said: "ta'ashaytu" and "ta'amaytu 'an al-shay'" (I feigned ignorance/blindness regarding the thing) when you neglect it as though you had not seen it. It is also said: "'ashawtu ila al-nar" (I squinted toward the fire) when you seek guidance from it with weak sight. This is of what is not to be heeded. Similar to it are 'ashiya and 'asha, meaning "'araja" (to be lame), with a kasra on the ra' for one who has the affliction, and "'araja" with a fatha for one who walks with the gait of a lame person without actual lameness, according to what is in the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari). There is a difference of opinion among the lexicographers on this. In the Qamus it is said: "'araja" with a fatha means when something has struck his leg and it is not innate; so if it is innate, then "'arija" like "fariha", or it may be vowelled with three vowels in what is not innate.

Zayd ibn Ali recited (ya'shu) with the long vowel (waw) retained. Al-Zamakhshari explained this on the basis that man is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), not a conditional jussive particle. It is also permitted that it be a conditional, and the long vowel is either for the sake of completion (ishba') or according to the dialect of one who apocopates a final weak verb by dropping the vowel, as reported by al-Akhfash. It is also permitted that the verb be jussive by dropping the nun, and the waw is the plural pronoun, the meaning of man having been observed in it. Al-Zamakhshari's explanation is based on the eloquent and regular, the most evident usage.

﴿Nuqayyid lahu shaytanan﴾ (We shall appoint for him a devil), that is, We shall send for him a devil to take control of him, the control of the yolk (qayd) over the egg-white, and it is the outer membrane (al-qishr al-a'la).

﴿Fahuwa lahu qarin﴾ (then he is his constant companion), constantly, never separating from him, never ceasing to whisper to him and mislead him. This is a punishment for disbelief, by sealing and by the absence of success, as it is said: Indeed Allah Most High punishes disobedience with an increase in the acquisition of misdeeds.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Ya'qub, Abu Amr in one report, Hammad from Asim, Isma from al-A'mash and from Asim, and al-Ulaymi from Abu Bakr recited (yuqayyid) with the ya', attributing it to the pronoun of (al-Rahman). Ibn Abbas recited (yuqayyad) with the ya' and the passive form, with (shaytan) in the nominative. The verb in all the recitations is jussive, and we have not heard that it was recited in the nominative. In the Kashshaf: whoever recited (man ya'shu) with the waw should have it in the nominative, meaning, on the basis of his explanation that man is a relative pronoun. On this basis it is also permitted that (yuqayyid) be nominative, but it is made quiescent for lightness.

In al-Bahr: it is permitted that (man) be a relative pronoun and (nuqayyid) be jussive, likening the relative pronoun to the conditional noun. And if that is heard with alladhi, which was never a conditional noun at all, then it is preferable that it be used as both relative and conditional. The poet said:

"Do not dig a well intending a brother in it, for you will fall into it yourself, not him."

"Likewise he who oppresses people unjustly, the consequences of what he has done will befall him despite himself."

Ibn al-A'rabi recited both of these. This is the view of the Kufan grammarians, and it has a basis in analogy: just as the relative pronoun is likened to the conditional noun, so that the particle fa' enters its predicate, so it is likened to it, and the predicate becomes jussive. However, the entry of fa' is regular when the predicate is a consequence of the relative clause, under its conditions mentioned in grammar; and the Basran grammarians do not analogize this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 37:

﴿And indeed they﴾ — i.e., the devils, each of whom is paired and assigned to each one of those who turn away (ya'shu) — ﴿surely bar them﴾ — i.e., they bar their companions, who are the disbelievers, referred to by "man ya'shu" (whoever turns away). The pronoun for "the devil" is plural because what is meant by it is the genus. The pronoun for "man" is plural in regard to meaning (ri'ayatan lil-ma'na), just as it was singular at first in regard to wording (ri'ayatan lil-lafz).

In al-Intisaf it is said that this verse contains two marvelous points (nukatan badi'atan). The first: it indicates that an indefinite noun (al-nakira) falling within the context of a conditional (shart) conveys generality ('umum). This is a question on which the usulis (jurists of legal theory) have disputed, and Imam al-Haramayn was among those who held that it conveys generality, until he corrected the Imams for their unqualified statement that an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is specific (takhussu). He said that the conditional is general, and an indefinite noun within its context is general. The jurist Abu al-Hasan 'Ali al-Abyari, the commentator on his book, refuted him vigorously. In this verse there is sufficient evidence for the Imam and for whoever holds his opinion, because the word "shaytan" is mentioned in it indefinitely within the context of a conditional, and we know that what is intended is the generality of devils, not a single one, for two reasons. One is that it is established that every person has a devil, so how much more so the one who turns away from the remembrance of God Most High. The other is from the verse itself: the pronoun referring back to it is plural in His words, Most High: (and indeed they), for it refers to "the shaytan" in one view only. Were it not for the conditional's conveying the generality of inclusion, it would not be permissible without difficulty for a plural pronoun to refer back to it. This is a point at which those who oppose this opinion, upon hearing it, fall silent. The second point: in it there is a refutation of those who claim that a return of pronouns to the meaning of "man" prevents a return to its wording afterward, and who argue for this on the basis that it is a summary after an explanation, which is contrary to what is known of eloquence. Al-Kindi and others have refuted that with verses, and my grandfather derived from this verse a refutation of that as well, because the pronoun returns to the wording in "yah'shu. Lahu" and to the meaning in "li-yasuddunahum," then again to the wording in "hatta idha ja'ana." I have previously stated that whoever prohibits this may have restricted his prohibition to its occurrence in a single sentence, whereas when sentences are multiple and each is independent, that may not be prohibited. End.

However, that the pronoun of "innahum" refers to the devil in one view only is open to scrutiny. Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun of object in "wa-innahum la-yasuddunahum" refers to "man" according to meaning, and this is better than the pronoun of "innahum" referring to the devil, as Ibn 'Atiyya held, because of the coherence (tanasuq) of the pronouns in "innahum" and what follows it. So do not overlook this. ﴿from the path﴾ — the clear path, to which the mention of the Most Merciful calls. ﴿And they think﴾ — i.e., those who turn away — ﴿that they﴾ — i.e., the devils — ﴿are guided﴾, i.e., to that true path; otherwise they would not follow them. Or: and those who turn away think that they themselves are guided, for the belief that the devils are guided entails the belief that they are likewise, since their way is one.

It seems that Abu Hayyan prefers this view also for coherence, and the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of "yasuddun," by supposing a subject, or from its subject, or from both, because it contains the pronouns of both. That is: and indeed they bar them from the true way while they think that they are guided to it.

The form of the present tense in the four verbs indicates continuous, renewed continuation, in keeping with His the Exalted's saying: ﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. For although (ḥattā) (until) is an initial particle that introduces a conditional sentence, it necessarily makes what follows its endpoint (ghāyah) for an extended matter. He used the singular pronoun in "jā'a" (came) and what follows it, because the intended meaning is to relate the statement of each one of those who turn away (al-ʿāshīn) to his companion (qarīn), to magnify the matter and make the state appalling. The meaning is: the state of those who turn away continues as mentioned, until, when each one of them comes to Us together with his companion on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿he says﴾, addressing him: ﴿"Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!"﴾, that is, in the world. It was also said: in the Hereafter. ﴿The distance of the two easts﴾, that is, the distance of each of them from the other. By the two are meant the east (mashriq) and the west (maghrib), as al-Zajjāj or al-Farrāʾ and others chose; but the east (mashriq) predominated over the west (maghrib), and they were dualized like al-Mawṣilayn (the two places: Mosul and al-Jazīrah), and the distance was attributed to them. The original would be "the distance of the east from the west and the west from the east." This elaborated form has been abbreviated only to avoid confusion, since it is clear that their distance is not meant from one single thing, because the distance of one from the other is nearness to the other; and because they are opposites, the distance of one from the other is like the utmost extent of distance, not their distance from some other thing. The implication of the context toward hyperbole is not denied, so there is no ambiguity from this aspect either. Ibn al-Sāʾib said: there is no predominance; the intended meaning is the sunrise point of the sun on the shortest day of the year and its sunrise point on the longest day of it. ﴿How evil a companion!﴾, that is, you [are]. It was also said: that is, he [is]; on the basis that it is part of the speech of Him the Exalted; but this is, as you see, [far-fetched].

Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Abu Bakr, the two Ḥaramīs (Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir... [as read by the two of Mecca and Medina]), Qatādah, al-Zuhrī and al-Jaḥdarī read (jāʾānā) in the dual, that is, al-ʿāshī and the qarīn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 39:

Page 83
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it will not benefit you﴾ etc. is a report of what will be said to them then, from Allah, mighty and majestic, as rebuke and reproach. The subject of (yanfa'a-kum, "it will benefit you") is a concealed pronoun referring to what is understood from what came before, i.e. "it will not benefit you" — that is, your wishing (tamannikum) for distance from them, or the regret (al-nadam), or the aforementioned statement. ﴿Today﴾, i.e. the Day of Resurrection, ﴿since you wronged﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿today﴾, i.e. "since it became clear that you wronged [yourselves] in the world." This was said by more than one scholar, and this is explained as "becoming clear" (al-tabayyun). It was said that this is so as not to raise the difficulty of making it, a past tense verb, a substitute for ﴿today﴾, which is future, since the becoming clear of their being wrongdoers in their own estimation only happens on the Day of Resurrection, so "today" and the time of becoming clear are one. This is like his saying:

"When we claim descent, a base woman has not borne me"

It was objected that the question remains, because (idh) is an adverb for past time, and it does not leave that by considering the becoming clear. Some scholars answered the difficulty by saying that idh may leave the past to the future, according to a group of scholars including Ibn Malik, citing the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So they will come to know﴾ ﴿when the shackles [are around their necks]﴾, and to the present, as some scholars held, citing the saying of the Glorified: ﴿And you do not do any deed except that We are witnesses over you when you are engaged in it﴾. So here it should be for the future. The grammarians weaken the claim that it leaves the past.

Al-Jalabi said: "Perhaps the more apparent is to take it as causal, so that it relates to the negation. Sibawayh said it has the meaning of causation and is a particle equivalent to the causal lam." Indeed, the majority denied this category, but Sibawayh's affirmation of it suffices as proof, as in the line:

"Indeed the saying is what Hadhdham said"

It was criticized: Sibawayh's affirmation alone is not enough to explain the speech of Allah, the Glorified, while all the imams of Arabic agree against it. Also, making the negation causal after it distances it. Abu Hayyan said: the substitution is not permitted if idh remains in its original sense of being an adverb for past time. If it is made to mean absolute time, it is permitted, but it is clear that this is a metaphor. Is the substitution sufficient as a clue to it? If it suffices, then so be it. Ibn Jinni said: I reviewed this question with Abu 'Ali, meaning the aforementioned substitution, many times, and the final outcome of it was that this world and the Hereafter are connected, and they are equal in the judgment and knowledge of Allah, the Glorified; time does not pass over Him, mighty and majestic, so it is as if idh is future or ﴿today﴾ is past, and that is correct. It was countered that what is considered is the state of narration, and the speech concerning it comes in accordance with what the Arabs customarily use; and were it not so, the doors of subtle points would be closed and considerations would be lost in expressions, and such a matter is too clear to need explanation. Abu al-Baqa said: the estimate is "after idh wronged you," so the genitive construction was deleted because it is known. Al-Hawfi said: idh is connected to what the meaning indicates, as if it were said: "And your gathering will not benefit you today, since you wronged, for example."

Some people raised a difficulty about the verse in that it contains the operation of ﴿yanfa'a-kum﴾, which indicates the future, being joined with lan, on ﴿today﴾, which is the present time, and idh, which is for past time. It was answered that the second is removed by what they estimated of becoming clear, since the becoming clear of the situation happens in the future; and the first, that ﴿today﴾ is defined for specificity, and it is the Day of Resurrection, not for presence, like the definition of "now," even if it is a kind of it.

It was said: it is removed by saying that the future is relative to the time of address, which is part of the times of the day, and it is as you see, so consider this and do not be heedless.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you, in the punishment, will be sharers﴾ is a cause for the negation of benefit, i.e. because it is your due that you and your companions share in the punishment, just as you were sharers in its cause in the world.

It is permitted that the verb be attributed to it, i.e. "your being sharers in the punishment will not benefit you, as the sharing of those who are in a difficult matter benefits them by their cooperation in bearing its burdens and dividing its severity and hardship; for each one of you bears of the punishment what his capacity cannot reach." Or "that will not benefit you in terms of consolation, for the one in distress is consoled and refreshed by finding a sharer in it, and this is what al-Khansa meant by her saying:"

"The rising of the sun reminds me of Sakhr, and I remember him at every sunset"

"Were it not for the great number of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself. They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him by consolation."

So these are consoled by their sharing, though it does not refresh them because of how great what they are in is. Or "that will not benefit you in terms of satisfaction (al-tashaffi)," i.e. you will not attain satisfaction by your companions being punished like you, since you used to pray against them by your saying: ﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment of the Fire﴾ and your saying: ﴿So give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾, so that you might be satisfied by that. The first of these three aspects was objected to on the grounds that benefiting from cooperation in bearing the burdens of punishment is not what occurs to their minds, so that it would be countered by its negation. It was answered that it is not far-fetched that this occurs to their minds, because of the closeness of association and companionship; the drowning man clutches at grass, and the thirsty man takes the mirage for water.

Ibn 'Amir read (innakum) with a kasra on the hamza, and this strengthens what was mentioned first of the concealment of the subject and the estimate of the lam in (anna-kum) both in meaning and in wording, because it is not possible for it to be the subject, so concealment is required; and because the sentence with it becomes a causal resumption, so it suits estimating the lam, so that the two readings agree.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind,﴾ is a rhetorical denial expressing wonder (inkar ta'ajjub) at the notion that the Prophet (ﷺ) could be the one who has the power to guide them, when they have become accustomed to disbelief, have habituated themselves to it, and have become immersed in error, to the point that the blindness they have, along with their blindness that comes with deafness, has become fixed. ﴿And whoever is in manifest error﴾ is a coordination ('atf) with "the blind," considering the difference between the two descriptions, namely blindness and error, in terms of their meanings, even though they converge in their outcome. The focus of the denial is the firm settling and stability in extreme error, which is evident, with no suspicion of any deficiency on the part of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Therefore, there is an allusion in it that none can do that except Allah alone, by compulsion and constraint. The Prophet (ﷺ) had been striving hard in calling his people, while they increased only in misguidance and in feigning blindness to the signs of prophethood that they witness, and in feigning deafness to the clear verses of the Qur'an that they hear. So it was revealed: ﴿Can you...﴾ etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 41:

﴿Whether We take you away﴾ — that is, if We take you (in death) before We let you see their punishment, and thereby We heal your breast and the breasts of the believers, ﴿then indeed from them We will be avenging﴾ — without doubt, both in this world and in the Hereafter. Some scholars restricted it to the punishment of the Hereafter, based on the words of the Exalted in another verse: ﴿Or We make you die, and to Us they will be returned﴾. The Qur'an explains one part of itself by another; but what we have mentioned is more complete in benefit and more in accord with the unrestricted sense of "revenge" (intiqam). As for that verse, there is no mention of it there. The particle "ma" (ma) is additional, for emphasis, and it stands in the same position as the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) in bringing in the emphatic nun (al-nun al-mu'akkidah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 42:

﴿Or We shall show you that which We have promised them﴾: that is, "Or We intend to show you the punishment which We have promised them." ﴿For indeed We are over them omnipotent﴾, in such a way that there is no escape for them from beneath Our dominion and Our subjugation. The sense of "intention" (al-iradah) is taken here because it is more fitting with the mention of omnipotence (al-iqtidar) that follows. In the expression "promise" (al-wa'd), and given that He, glorified is He, does not break His appointment (al-mi'ad), there is an indication that it is what will certainly occur. And so it was: not one of their chieftains escaped at Badr and elsewhere, except those who took refuge in faith. It is also read (nuriyannaka) with the light nun (al-nun al-khafifah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 43:

﴿So hold fast to that which has been revealed to you; indeed you are upon a straight path.﴾ This is a consolation for him (ﷺ), and a command to him, peace be upon him, or to his community, to persist in holding fast to the verses and acting upon them. The fa' (the particle "fa") is in response to an elided conditional clause, meaning: if one of these two matters is inevitably occurring, then hold fast to that which We have revealed to you. ﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, what was revealed to you, and by it is meant the Qur'an, ﴿is a reminder﴾, a great honour, ﴿for you and for your people﴾. Their people are the Quraysh, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, "from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: 'I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he said: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, knew what was in my heart of love for my people, so He gave me glad tidings concerning them, and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, the verse, and He made the reminder and the honour for my people in His Book.' Until he said: "Adi said: I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Quraysh were mentioned in his presence with good, except that it pleased him, until the joy would appear on his face for all the people. It has also been said that "your people" means the Arabs in general, since the Qur'an was revealed in their language; then this honour is specified further for those who are closest, so that the honour belongs to the Quraysh more than to others, then to the Banu Hashim more than to the rest of the Quraysh. In a report from Qatadah, it is said that "your people" are those who followed him (ﷺ) from among his community.

al-Hasan said: "They are the community (ummah), and the meaning is: indeed it is a reminder and an admonition for you and for your community." The view I find more preferable is the first opinion.

﴿And you will be questioned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection about it and about your fulfilment of its rights. al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: you will be questioned about giving thanks for the honour which Allah has given you. It has been said that this verse indicates that a person desires good praise and a good name, for if that were not desirable, Allah would not have bestowed it as a favour upon His Messenger (ﷺ). A good remembrance stands in place of life, and therefore it is said: "A young man's remembrance is his second life." Ibn Duraid said:

"Man is only a story after him,
so be a good story for whoever is aware."

Another said:

"Worldly life is only its good qualities,
the goodness of what remains of report."

It is related that the tyrant Hulagu asked his companions: "Who is the king?" They said to him: "You are the one who subdued the lands and ruled the earth, and the kings obeyed you." The muezzin, who was calling the adhan at that time, said: "No, the king is the one who died more than six hundred years ago, and he is mentioned on the minarets every day and night five times. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 43, verse 45:**

﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾ That is, did We ever decree the worship of other than Allah, glorified is He? And did it appear in the religion (*milla*) of any of the messengers, upon them be peace? The purpose is to cite the consensus (*ijma'*) of the messengers upon *tawhid* (monotheism, the oneness of God), and to alert that this is not a novelty (*bid'a*) that the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, invented, so that he should be denied and opposed for it. The speech is either according to an omitted noun, meaning "ask the communities of those whom We sent," or the asking of the communities is treated as the asking of the messengers to whom they were sent.

Al-Farra' said: "They only report from the books of the messengers. So when he asks them, it is as if he asked the messengers, upon them be peace." According to both interpretations, the one asked is the communities. This was narrated from al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ata', and it is also a report from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others recorded from Qatada that in some recitations it reads: "And ask those to whom We sent Our messengers before you."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Sa'id ibn Mansur recorded from Mujahid, who said: "Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) used to recite: *And ask those to whom We sent messengers before you.*" And from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited: *And ask those who read the Book before you, from among the believers of the People of the Book.* Some scholars took the asking to be a metaphor for looking into and investigating their religions, like the expression in poetry about asking abandoned campsites and ruins and the like, as in their saying: "Ask the earth who split your rivers, planted your trees, and gathered your fruits."

It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Zayd that the speech is on its apparent meaning, and that it was said to the Prophet, upon him be peace, on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), when the prophets were gathered for him in al-Bayt al-Muqaddas (Jerusalem). So understand. He, upon him be peace, did not ask them, since he was not in doubt.

It is related in some reports that Mika'il said to Jibril, upon them both be peace: "Did Muhammad, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, ask about this?" He replied: "He is greater in certainty and firmer in faith than to ask." This view has been criticized on the grounds that the purpose of this question is to confront the polytheists, who deny the Isra', and there is room for discussion about it. The address, according to all that you have heard, is to our Prophet, upon him be peace.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), what appears is that it is an address to the listener who wishes to investigate the religions. It was said to him: "Ask, O observer, the followers of the messengers: Did their messengers bring the worship of other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic? For they will inform you that this did not occur, and it is not possible for them to have brought it." By my life, this is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning. Among the things that are astonishing is what has been said: the meaning is "ask me," or "ask us about those whom We sent," and the verb *is'al* is suspended (*mu'allaq*), so *man* is raised, being an interrogative noun in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtada'*), and *arsalna* is its predicate. The clause is in the accusative position governed by *is'al* after the omission of the preposition, as if his asking was: "O Lord, whom You sent before me of Your messengers, did You make the worship of gods part of their mission?" Then the asking was reported, and the address was returned to the Prophet, upon him be peace, in the Exalted words *from before you* (*min qablika*). End of quotation. Let whoever reads "Abu Jad" ask: would he be pleased with this speech, and would he approve of interpreting the glorious words of Allah the Exalted in this way?

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 46:**

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾, being accompanied by them, ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, the nobles of his people. They are singled out for mention because the rest of them were followers. ﴿And he said﴾ to them, ﴿"Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ sent to you. The purpose of relating this account is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to refute their statement: ﴿"Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?"﴾ Because Moses (peace be upon him), despite his lack of worldly ornaments, had, in the face of Pharaoh, who was a tyrannical king, no such wealth, yet Allah, glorified is He, supported him with His revelation and with what He sent down to him. The citation of his call (peace be upon him) to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), following what has been indicated about the ijma' (consensus) of all the messengers (peace be upon them) upon it, makes clear the connection of these verses to what precedes them.

Abu Hayyan said: their connection is in two respects. The first is that He mentioned earlier the statement of the polytheists, ﴿"Why was this not sent down..."﴾ etc., and in it is the assumption that greatness lies in rank and wealth. In these verses it is indicated that Pharaoh had already embraced such a notion, in his saying: ﴿"Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?"﴾ etc. So he is their precedent in this, and he was taken to account for it; likewise they will be taken to account. The second is that when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿"And ask"﴾ etc., He mentioned the story of Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them both), who have more followers than those of the prophets who preceded them, and each of them brought tawhid. There was nothing in what they brought that permitted taking gods besides Allah, as Quraysh had done. Therefore the mention of their story suits the verse that precedes it.

[p. 87]

﴿Then when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them.﴾ That is, the laughing at them took them by surprise; that is, they mocked them as soon as they saw them, without reflecting on them. In *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary), he says: it is permissible for *lammā* (لَمّا, "when/as soon as") to be answered by *idhā al-mufājaʾa* (إذا المفاجأة, the "idhā of sudden surprise"), because a verb of surprise (*fiʿl al-mufājaʾa*, فعل المفاجأة) is implied with it, and it is the governing element of the accusative case in its position, as if it were said: "When he brought them Our signs, they were suddenly at the time of their laughing." So the answer, in his view, is that implied verb, and it is the governor of *lammā*. It is taken to be in the past tense because that is the familiar form in its answer. And *idhā* is an object (*mafʿūl bihi*, مفعول به), not an adverb of time (*ẓarf*, ظرف).

Abū Ḥayyān said: "I do not know of any grammarian who held what this man held, that *idhā al-fujāʾiyya* is in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose estimate is *fājaʾa* (he surprised). Rather, there are three views on it.

The first: it is a particle (*ḥarf*), so it does not need a governor.

The second: it is an adverb of place (*ẓarf makān*). If, after the noun following it, a predicate is stated, that predicate is what governs it, as in: *kharajtu fa-idhā Zaydun qāʾimun* ("I went out, and behold, Zayd was standing"). Here *qāʾim* is what governs it, and the sense is: "I went out, and in the place where I went out, Zayd was standing."

The third: it is an adverb of time (*ẓarf zamān*), and the governor of it is also the predicate, as if it were said: "Then in the time when I went out, Zayd was standing."

If no predicate is mentioned after the noun, or a noun in the accusative of state (*ḥāl*) is mentioned, then *idhā* is the predicate of the subject (*khabar lil-mubtadaʾ*). If it is a solid entity (*juththa*, جثة), and we say that *idhā* is an adverb of place, the matter is clear. If we say it is an adverb of time, the sentence requires the omission of a modifier (*ḥadhf muḍāf*), that is: "Then in the time there is the presence of Zayd."

Moreover, the surprise he claims does not indicate that it arises from the preceding speech; rather, the meaning indicates that it arises from the speech in which it occurs. You say: *kharajtu fa-idhā al-asadu* ("I went out, and behold, a lion"), meaning: "then the lion surprised me." End of quotation."

And al-Khafājī said: what has been said, that its accusative governance is by the implied verb of surprise in this way, no grammarian has said it, so it is not to be considered. Its detailed treatment is in the commentaries on *al-Mughnī* (Ibn Hishām's *Mughni al-Labīb*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 48:

﴿And We did not show them any sign⁠﴾ from among the signs,

﴿except that it was greater than its sister⁠﴾, i.e., a sign like it in being a sign indicating prophethood. It has been objected that this implies each of the signs being both superior and inferior at the same time, which leads to contradiction, and to preferring a thing over itself, given the generality of "a sign" in the negation. It was answered that the purpose of this statement is that they are all described as being great, such that they do not much differ in this respect, in the sense that each one, for its completeness in itself, when considered, is said to be greater than the rest, because of its independence in conveying the intended meaning fully, as the poet al-Hamasi said:

Whomever you meet among them, you will say: I have met their leader,
like the stars by which the night traveler journeys.

And when the whole is considered, one stops from preferring among them. Fatimah bint Khurshub al-Anmariyyah indeed favored among her sons the perfect ones: Rabi'ah al-Huffaz, Imarah al-Wahhab, and Uns al-Fawaris. Then she said: "I have seen their ranks close to one another, with little difference. May I be bereaved of them if I knew which of them is best. They are like a hoop of which no one knows where its ends are."

Some of the eminent scholars said: The intent of the comparative form (af'al) is increase in one respect, i.e., "We do not show them any sign except that it is specially characterized by a type of miraculousness, superior to others by that consideration." There is no harm in one thing being both superior and inferior by two considerations. Jalal al-Din al-Dawani has discussed this at length in his glosses on the New Commentary to al-Tajrid, so whoever wants it should refer to them.

In al-Bahr it is said: His signs, upon him be peace, were among the great signs, and each one was greater than the one before it. Accordingly, there is a deleted qualifier, i.e., "greater than its sister preceding it," and there is then no contradiction in the speech. This ruling does not apply to the first sign, since nothing preceded it, so that it would be greater than it. Some scholars also mentioned regarding the comparative of greatness that the first sign requires one knowledge, and the second requires knowledge added to the knowledge of the first, so the return increases. End quote. The former explanation is preferable, because the intended meaning is common in such a construction.

﴿And We seized them with punishment⁠﴾, such as the years of drought, the locusts, the lice, and others:

Page 88

﴿so that they might return⁠﴾, i.e., in order that they might return and repent from the disbelief they were upon.

﴿And they said, "O sorcerer!"﴾ The majority of scholars said: this is a form of address of honour, since they used to call the learned and skilled man "sorcerer" because of their esteem for the knowledge of sorcery (sihr). This is related by al-Tabarsi in *Majma' al-Bayan* from al-Kalbi and al-Jubba'i. It was also said that the meaning is "O overcomer of the sorcerers," derived from *sāḥarahu fa-saḥarahu*, like *khāṣamahu fa-khaṣamahu* ("he disputed with him and overcame him in the dispute"). So this too is a form of address of honour. It was also said that "sorcerer" carries its usual meaning, and that they had become accustomed to calling him that before, and that the situation of asking him to supplicate on their behalf required that they not address him by it, but that because of their extreme distress their tongues slipped into what they were accustomed to. It was also said that this is an address of mockery and disparagement, prompted by the intensity of their stubbornness and their great foolishness. This is related from al-Hasan.

Al-Zamakhshari answered the apparent contradiction between this address and their later statement, ﴿Indeed we are surely guided﴾, by saying that this statement was a promise they intended to break and a firm pledge they resolved to violate, conditional upon his supplicating for them and the punishment being lifted from them. But it may be objected that although the promise was intended to be broken, the显 manifestation of breaking it while they were humbly entreating him (peace be upon him) is incompatible with that, because they were seeking to soften his heart (peace be upon him).

It was also said that the more apparent view is that they said, "O Moses," as in *al-A'raf*, but God, exalted is He, related their words here according to their state and in accordance with what was in their hearts, to condemn that and to console His beloved (ﷺ). On this view, it is the reverse of His statement, may He be glorified, ﴿Indeed we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the Messenger of God﴾. Their later statement is taken as a summary of what was detailed there regarding faith and the sending of the Children of Israel, so there is no need to hold that the two statements were made in two separate gatherings in order to reconcile what is mentioned here with what is mentioned there. This view is not free from remoteness, though I see no harm in the aforementioned hypothesis. It is also read as (*yā ayyuhu*) with a *ḍamma* on the *hā'*.

﴿Pray to your Lord for us﴾ that He remove the punishment from us, ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾, that is, by His covenant with you. The intended meaning is prophethood. It is called a covenant (*ʿahd*) either because God, exalted is He, made a covenant with His Prophet (peace be upon him) that He would honour him with it, and the Prophet made a covenant with his Lord, glorified is He, that he would bear its burdens, or because of the hardship involved in shouldering its burdens and the special bond between them, as between two parties to a covenant; or because it has rights that must be preserved, just as a covenant is preserved; or it is from the sense of the *ʿahd* that is written for governors, as though prophethood were a decree from God, exalted is He, appointing the one whom He honoured with it. The *bāʾ* (in *bi-mā*) is either attached to *udʿu* (pray), or it is related to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in it, meaning: seeking nearness to Him, exalted is He, by what He covenanted; or to an omitted element indicated by their entreaty, such as "grant us relief in what we seek." It may also be an oath, with the answer being what follows. On this reading it is a true oath, and on the previous reading it is an oath of entreaty (*al-qasam al-istiʿṭāfī*, an oath used to win compassion). On the first reading it denotes causation. Including this within entreaty is a departure from technical usage. It is also permissible that the covenant means the covenant of answering the supplication, as if it were said: by what God, exalted is He, has covenanted to you, honouring you, of answering your call, or what He covenanted regarding the lifting of punishment from those who are guided. The function of the *bāʾ* in both cases is as explained above. It is also permissible that the covenant means faith and obedience, meaning: by what He covenanted with you, and you fulfilled it, taking *ʿahida ilayhi* to mean "he required of him a pledge to do such-and-such," i.e., he took from him a pledge to perform it. From this comes the covenant written for governors. The phrase *ʿindaka* ("with you") suffices in place of mentioning the relative clause, while also conveying that it is preserved and stored with the one addressed. On this reading, it is better for *mā* to be a relative pronoun. As al-Kashshaf says, this reading contains, in wording, meaning and context, a remoteness that is not hidden from the discerning.

﴿Indeed we are surely guided﴾, that is, we are believers firmly upon faith. This is either conditional upon the lifting of the punishment, as in their stated words in *Surat al-A'raf*: ﴿If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you﴾, or it is unconditional, in which case this must have been said by them in another gathering. Even if we say that their request for supplication occurred only once or more than once, but in one uniform manner, it has been said here that they meant by being guided: faith and the sending of the Children of Israel, as you have just heard.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 50:

﴿So when We removed the punishment from them﴾ i.e., in response to his supplication. So in the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e., he supplicated to Us for the removal of the punishment, so We removed it; then when We had removed it from them, ﴿behold, they broke their word﴾. The breaking of their covenant to be guided surprised them, or they were surprised at the time of breaking their covenant. Abu Haywah recited (yankithun) with a kasra on the kaf.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 51:**

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying: "O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me?"﴾ That is, he raised his voice himself, among his people, with this statement. Perhaps he had gathered the nobles of the Copts in the place where he was, after the punishment was lifted, and so he proclaimed among them with this, so that his words would spread among all the Copts and would become great in their souls, lest they believe in Musa, peace be upon him, and abandon him.

It is also permissible that the attribution of the proclaiming (*nida'*) to him is figurative (*majaz*), and that what is meant is that he ordered the proclamation of this in the markets, the alleys, and the gathering places of people. This is like saying "the emir built the city."

﴿And proclaimed﴾: it has been said that it is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the implied *fajaa* (suddenly). It took the status of an intransitive verb, and it was made transitive by *fi* (in), as in the saying of the poet: "He cuts into their hamstrings with my blade" (*yajrahu fi 'araqibiha nasli*). This indicates the establishment of the proclamation among them.

By "the kingdom of Egypt" he meant its control and its authority over it through rule. He did not mean Egypt itself, but rather it and what follows it, from Alexandria to Aswan, as is mentioned in *al-Bahr*. "The rivers" are the canals that branch out from the blessed Nile, such as the Canal of the King, the Damietta branch, and the Tinnis branch. Perhaps the Tulun branch was among them at that time, but it became obliterated, so Ahmad ibn Tulun, king of Egypt in Islam, renewed it. By his saying ﴿from beneath me﴾ he meant from beneath my command.

Others than one have said: there were rivers that branched out from the Nile and flowed beneath his palace while he overlooked them. It was said: he had a great, elevated throne beneath which flowed rivers that he had drawn out from the Nile. Qatada said: he had gardens and orchards before him through which the rivers flowed. Al-Dahhak interpreted "the rivers" as the commanders, the leaders, and the tyrants. The meaning of their flowing beneath him is that they march under his banner and obey his command. But this is far-fetched. Likewise, whoever interpreted them as wealth, and whoever interpreted them as horses, saying: just as a horse is called a sea, it is called a river. Rather, these three interpretations come close to the interpretations of the Batiniyya, so one should not turn to them.

The *waw* in ﴿and these﴾ and what follows is either coordinating (*'atifa*), coordinating these rivers with the kingdom, so the clause *tajri* ("flow") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of them; or it is for the circumstance (*lil-hal*), so *hadhihi* is the subject (*mubtada'*), *al-anhar* is a descriptive adjective (*sifa*) or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*), the clause *tajri* is the predicate (*khabar*) of the subject, and the clause "these..." etc. is a circumstantial clause from the first-person pronoun. It is also permissible that it be coordinating: *wa-hadhihi tajri* is a subject and predicate, and the clause is coordinated on the noun of *laysa* and its predicate.

His saying ﴿Do you not then see?﴾ is with an implied object, meaning: do you not then see that, that is, what has been mentioned. It is also permissible that it be treated as intransitive, and the meaning is: do you not have sight or insight? Isa read *tubsirun* with a kasra on the *nun*, so the *ya'* that is the object is omitted. Fahd ibn al-Saqr read *yubsirun* with the *ya'* of the third person, mentioned in *al-Kamil* for al-Hazli and al-Saji, from Ya'qub, mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh.

It is not hidden how vast the distance is between the accursed one's boasting of the kingdom of Egypt and his claim to lordship. It is related from al-Rashid that when he recited this verse he said: "I shall appoint over it (meaning Egypt) the lowliest of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, and he was in a state of ablution. It is related from Abd Allah ibn Tahir that he was appointed over it, and went out to it. When he approached it and his eye fell upon it, he said: "This is the town that Pharaoh boasted of, until he said: ﴿Does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me?﴾ By God, it is less in my estimation than that I should enter it," and he turned his reins back.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 52:

﴿Am ana khayrun﴾ (Or am I not better), despite this expansiveness and abundance in dominion and wealth, ﴿than this one who is despicable﴾, that is, weak and contemptible, or lowly and abased. He is from the *muhanah* (contemptibility), which means paucity or humiliation. ﴿And he can hardly express himself clearly﴾, that is, his speech. The majority hold that he, peace be upon him, had some impediment in his tongue as a result of the ember, but the accursed one exaggerated.

As for those who hold that God, exalted is He, had answered his supplication and untied the knot in his tongue so that no trace of it remained, they said: the meaning of ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ is that he cannot clearly present his proof that indicates the truth of what he claims, not that he has no ability to speak clearly. This is a slander against him, peace be upon him. Do you not see his debate with him, his refutation of him, and his silencing of him? It was also said: he reproached him with the stammer that he had, peace be upon him, during the days when he was with him. The accursed one meant that he, peace be upon him, did not have with him the number of followers and the instruments of kingship and governance by which he could be supported, and that he was himself deficient in what men are described as having: eloquence and clarity of speech.

﴿Am﴾ (or), according to what is reported from Sibawayh and al-Khalil, is *muttasilah* (connective, linking two alternatives). The cause has been placed after its effect, in the sense of the *musabbab*, according to what al-Zamakhshari held. The meaning is: "Will you not see? Or do you see?" However, he placed ﴿Am ana khayrun﴾ in the position of "Or do you see?"

The clarification of this is that Pharaoh, may the curse be upon him, when he presented the causes of his expansiveness and leadership by his saying ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?﴾ and so on, followed it with his saying ﴿Will you not see?﴾, to belittle them and to alert them that it is so clear that it is not hidden from one who has two eyes. He said in its counterpart: ﴿Or am I not better?﴾, meaning: "Or do you see that I am the one who is preeminent and followed?" In this deviation there is an indication that this alternative is the one that is undoubtedly accepted by you. He is thus relating it as it is in their own speech after they had seen it. This is a wondrous style and a strange art.

Al-Zamakhshari made it an instance of placing the cause in the position of the effect, because his being better in himself, that is, his having the causes of precedence that bring about that, and the kingship, is a cause for it to be said of him, "You are better than him." Their saying, "You are better," is a cause for their being perceptive. The cause of a cause may also be called a cause, so there is no objection to the claim that the cause is their saying "You are better," not his saying "I am better."

Al-Qadi al-Baydawi said: it is from placing the effect in the position of the cause, because their knowledge that he is better is derived from seeing. Against this it is said that what is mentioned is "I am better," not "Do you know that I am better?" He may respond: that suffices for its purpose, because he made what they have a known and accepted matter, so he said ﴿Or am I not better?﴾ and not "Or do you know," as has passed. It is not hidden that what al-Zamakhshari mentioned is more apparent. Thus it is in *al-Kashshaf*.

The Allamah al-Thani, in explaining this, said: his saying "I am better" is a cause for their saying from the aspect of prompting them to reflect on his circumstances and his readiness for what he claims. Their saying "You are better" is a cause for their being perceptive in his sight. So "I am better" is a cause of it indirectly. But it is not hidden that it is a cause for knowledge of that and for judging it. As for existence, the matter is the reverse, because their perceiving is the cause of his saying "You are better." So consider this.

In sum, what follows ﴿am﴾ is interpreted as a verbal sentence, which is linked in form and meaning to what you have heard and similar things, in terms of interpretation: ﴿Did you call them, or are you silent?﴾, that is, or have you been silent? And the poet's saying:

*Amukhdiju al-yadayni am atammat*
(Is he one with deficient hands, or complete?), that is, or is he complete?

It was also said that the counterpart was omitted because the meaning indicates it, and the estimate is: "Will you not see? Or do you see that I am better," and so on. This was criticised on the grounds that it is not permissible unless it comes after *am* with *la* (not), as in *ayaqumu Zaydun am la* (Does Zayd stand, or not?), meaning: or does he not stand. As for omitting it without *la*, it is not part of their speech. It was also permitted that there is an omission in the speech following the method of *al-ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which two parallel elements are mentioned and each omits what is mentioned in the other), and the meaning is: "Is he better than me? Then do you not see what I reminded you of? Or am I better than him?" because you see it. This should not be given attention.

Many others permitted that ﴿am﴾ is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive), estimated as *bal* (rather), with the interrogative hamzah that is used for affirmation, as if the accursed one said, after enumerating the causes of his superiority and the beginnings of his preeminence: "Is it established and fixed with you that I am better, and this is my state, as opposed to this one?" Some preferred this because it avoids the strain of estimating a counterpart that is necessarily required first, in order to be good in the connective case.

Al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubaydah said: ﴿am﴾ means *bal* (rather), so he has moved from that speech to informing them that he is better, like the poet's saying:

*Badat mithla qarni al-shamsi fi rawnaqi al-duha*
*Wa suratuha am anta fi al-'ayni amlahu*
(She appeared like the horn of the sun in the splendor of the forenoon, and her form, or rather you, is more beautiful in the eye.)

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is disjunctive in form and connective in meaning, and he meant the interpretation that has passed. There is no contradiction in this with what the grammarians have agreed upon, as is supposed.

The sentence ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ is either conjoined to the relative clause, or is a new sentence, or is a circumstantial clause.

It is also read *Ama ana khayrun* (Am I not better?), with the hamzah introduced before the negative *ma*. Al-Baqir, may God be pleased with him, read *yabinu* with a fatha on the ya, from *ban*, meaning "to become manifest" when it appears clearly.
