Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 53:

﴿So why were not bracelets of gold cast upon him?﴾ This is a metaphor (kinayah) for granting him rulership. Mujahid said: "When they made a man their chief, they would adorn him with two bracelets and put a gold collar around his neck, as a sign of his lordship."

Page 91

Pharaoh said: "Why has the Lord of Musa not cast upon him bracelets of gold, if he is truthful?" This is from the accursed one, for he assumed that leadership (riyasah) is a necessary consequence of prophethood (risalah), just as the disbelievers of Quraysh said regarding "the great man of the two cities." The word al-asawirah is the plural of siwar, like khimar and akhmirah. Al-A'mash read (asawir), and it is transmitted from Ubayy, and from Abu 'Amr, as the plural of asawirah, so it is the plural of a plural. The majority read (asawirah), the plural of asawar, meaning siwar (bracelet), and the ta' marbutah is a substitute for the yaa' of asawir, for in a plural whose extra letter has been dropped, the ta' is a compensation for it, as in zanadiqah, the plural of zindiq.

Abdullah and Ubayy, according to the well-known narration, read (asawir). Al-Dahhak read alqa in the active voice, meaning God Most High cast (alqa) asawiratan with an accusative ending. ﴿Or the angels came with him, accompanying him﴾ from qarantuhu bihi, so he accompanied. It was interpreted as "joined with him" (maqrunin), i.e., attached to him, because that meaning is necessarily implied by this reading. It was also interpreted as "successive together" (mutaqarinin) from iqtarana in the sense of taqarana, and the idiom iqtiran is a metaphor or a metonymy for assistance.

Accordingly Ibn Abbas said: "They help him against whoever opposes him." It was also said: "in confirmation (of him)." Had it not been so, mentioning it after his saying "with him" would serve no purpose. The first meaning is sensory (hissi), and the second is abstract (ma'nawi). It was also said: mutaqarinin in the sense of mujtami'in kathirin (gathered in large numbers), and from Qatadah: mutatabi'in (following one another in succession).

﴿So he made light of his people﴾, that is, he asked them for lightness in obeying him, taking the *sin* (the particle *sīn* in *istakhaff*, indicating seeking) in its literal sense of requesting. The meaning of *khiffah* (lightness) is swiftness in responding to him and following him, as one says *hum khufūf* ("they are quick") when they are called. This is a well-known metaphor (*majāz*). Ibn al-A'rābī said: *istakhaffa aḥlāmahum* means he found their minds light, i.e., their intellects were few and weak. So the form *istif'āl* here indicates finding (*wijdān*), like *af'ala*, as one says *aḥmadtuhu* ("I found him praiseworthy"). Attributing this to the people involves a figurative usage (*tajawwuz*).

﴿So they obeyed him﴾ in what he commanded them, ﴿indeed they were a people who were defiantly disobedient﴾. Therefore they hastened to obey that corrupt, wicked deviator.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 55:

﴿فَلَمّا آسَفُونا﴾ i.e., made Us angry, as ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face) said. And in its meaning is what has been said: i.e., they made Us angry with the utmost anger, that is, by their deeds.

Anger (al-ghadab) according to the later scholars (al-khalaf) is a metaphor for the will to punish, so it is an attribute of essence (sifat dhat); or it is a metaphor for the punishment itself, so it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l).

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Rida (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) said: Indeed Allah, glorified is He, does not feel regret (ya'saf) as We feel it, but He has friends (awliya') who feel regret and are pleased, so He, glorified is He, made their pleasure His pleasure and their anger His anger, the Exalted. On this basis the Mighty and Majestic said: "Whoever humiliates a friend of Mine has declared war against Me," and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. And upon this it has been said: the meaning is "when they made Musa, peace be upon him, and those with him feel regret." The early scholars (al-salaf) do not interpret; they say: anger in us is a psychological affect (infi'al nafsani), but His attributes, glorified is He, are not like Our attributes in any respect.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both) that the interpretation of asaf (regret) is sorrow (huzn), and that he said here: i.e., they grieved Our believing friends, such as the magicians and the Children of Israel.

Al-Raghib mentioned that asaf is sorrow and anger together, and it may be said of each of them separately. Its reality is the boiling of the heart's blood out of desire for revenge. When that is directed at one who is beneath him, it spreads and becomes anger; when it is directed at one who is above him, it contracts and becomes sorrow. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about the two, and he said: "Their source is one, but the wording differs. Whoever contends with one he is able to overpower shows it as rage and anger, and whoever contends with one he is not able to overpower shows it as grief and distress." With this consideration the poet said:

"The grief of every brother in grief is a brother to anger."

End quote. And according to all the opinions, āsafa is transmitted with a hamza from asifa.

﴿انْتَقَمْنا مِنهم فَأغْرَقْناهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ We took revenge upon them and drowned them all, in the sea (al-yamm).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 56:

﴿So We made them a precedent﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Qatada said: that is, those who go before (ilā al-nār), i.e., going ahead to the Fire.

Others said: "An example for the disbelievers who come after them, who follow their path in deserving a punishment like theirs and having it descend upon them." The speech is figurative (ʿalā al-istiʿāra), because the later generation follows the earlier one (al-salaf). So when they followed them in disbelief, it was as if they had followed them in the object of wrath (maʿlūl al-ghaḍab). It (salaf) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective (nuʿita bihi), and therefore its application to the few and the many is valid. It was also said: it is the plural of sālif, like ḥāris and ḥaras, and khādim and khadam. This may mean that the plural is intended in its apparent sense, and it may mean that the collective noun (ism al-jamʿ) is intended, since faʿal is not among the patterns of plurals, being predominant in singular nouns. The well-known plural of it is aslāf, and sulāf also occurs.

Abu ʿAbd Allah and his companions, Saʿid ibn ʿIyad, al-Aʿmash, al-Aʿraj, Talha, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (sulufan) with two ḍammas, the plural of salīf, like farīq, in both form and meaning. Al-Qasim ibn Maʿn heard the Arabs say: "A salīf of people has passed away," meaning a group of them. It was also said: it is the plural of salf, like ṣabr, the plural of ṣābir, or the plural of salaf, like janab.

ʿAli, may God honour his face, Mujahid and al-Aʿraj also read (sulafan) with a ḍamma then a fatḥa. This is either because the ḍamma on the lam was changed to a fatḥa for lightness, as is said of judud (with a ḍamma on the dal), judad (with a fatḥa), or because it is the plural of sulfa, meaning a community and group of people; that is, "We made them a community that has passed away." Sulaf, with a ḍamma then a fatḥa, outside this context, means the young of the ... (ḥāshiyya gap). The plural is silfān, like ṣirdān, and it may be pronounced with a ḍamma.

﴿And an example for the later ones﴾: that is, a lesson for them. The intended "they" are the disbelievers after them. The prepositional phrase is governed by the rule of contention (ʿalā al-tanāzuʿ) with salafan and mathalan. It is permissible for mathal to mean the wondrous story that travels like proverbs. The meaning of their being an example for the disbelievers is that it is said to them: "Your example is the example of the people of Pharaoh." It is also permissible for the prepositional phrase to be attached to the second term, and for "the later ones" to be generalised so as to include the believers. That they are a wondrous story for all is evident.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 57:

﴿And when the son of Mary was cited as an example﴾ etc. is an explanation of the obstinacy of the Quraysh in falsehood and a refutation of them. It is narrated that ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā, before his Islam, said to the Prophet (ﷺ), when he heard him recite: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾: "Do not the Christians worship the Messiah, while you say that he was a prophet, and a righteous servant among the servants of Allah the Exalted? If he is in the Fire, then we are pleased that we and our gods be with him." So the Quraysh rejoiced and laughed, and their voices rose. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿when your people thereof cry out﴾. The meaning, then, is: when Ibn al-Zibaʿrā cited ʿĪsā ibn Maryam as an example, and argued against you with the worship of the Christians of him, then your people, because of that and on account of it, raise a clamour and uproar in joy and dispute. Since the argument used to travel as proverbs travel in fame, it was called a mathal (example), or al-mathal is in the sense of al-mithāl (likeness), i.e., he made him a standard and a witness for the invalidation of his (ﷺ) statement: "Indeed, their gods are the fuel of Hell." And ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) made himself an example, in the manner of (al-ḥajju ʿArafah) ("the pilgrimage is ʿArafah").

Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Rajāʾ, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn ʿĀmir, Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī read (yaṣuddūna) with a ḍammah on the ṣād, from ṣudūd (turning away). This reading is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, denied this reading, and that was before its mass transmission (tawātur) reached him. The meaning according to it is: when your people, on account of that, turn away from the truth by disputing with a weak, feeble argument. It has also been said that the intended meaning is: they persist in what they were upon of turning away.

Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ said: yaṣiddūna with a kasrah and yaṣuddūna with a ḍammah are two dialects with one meaning, like yaʿrishūna and yaʿrushūna, and their meaning is yaḍijjūna (they clamour). It is also permitted that it means yuʿriḍūna (they turn away).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 58:**

﴿And they said﴾ as a preface to what they built upon of falsehood, which is embellished with that by which the foolish are deceived: ﴿Are our gods better, or he?﴾ That is, it is evident to you that ʿIsa (peace be upon him) is better than our gods; so, since he is in the Fire, there is no harm in their being in it along with us. The Kufans realized both hamzas, the interrogative hamza and the original hamza, while the remaining seven [readers] eased the second one to an intermediate sound (bayn bayn),
Page 93
and Warsh, in the narration of Abu al-Azhar, read it with a single hamza in the form of a declarative statement. The apparent view is that this is by omitting the interrogative hamza. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They did not strike it for you except as a dispute. Rather, they are a contentious people﴾ is a general refutation of their falsehood, relying on what was detailed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the good [reward] has preceded﴾, and as an alert that its falsehood is something that is not hidden from anyone who has a little sense, so how [could it be hidden] from others? But stubbornness blinds and deafens. That is: they did not strike that for you except for the sake of disputation and quarrelling, not to seek the truth, for it is in the extreme of falsehood. Rather, they are a people of fierce, strong contention, disposed to a *mahk* (i.e., asking for the creation's [attention]) and obstinacy. So *jadalan* is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). It was also said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning "disputing." Ibn Muqsim read *jidalan* with a kasra on the *jim* and an alif after the *dal*.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He is not but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour﴾, i.e., Jesus, son of Mary, was nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favour by prophethood (nubuwwah) and its attendant gifts. So he is exalted in rank according to his measure, but he has no share of the right to be worshipped (istihqaq al-ma'budiyyah). This is a wise statement that contains what is contained in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us﴾, but by way of allusion, and as a refutation of the view of the Christians in preferring his worship (peace be upon him), as an indirect reference to the Quraysh's worship of other than Him, Glorified and Exalted is He. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made him an example﴾, i.e., a wondrous matter, worthy that his mention spread like the circulating proverbs, ﴿for the Children of Israel﴾, in that We created him without a father, and gave him the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind-born and the leper, and the like, which We did not give to anyone else in his time. This is a statement in which is summarized the aspect over which people were tested regarding him and by him, and the aspect of its indication of the power of his Creator, exalted is His majesty, and (it is stated) after clarifying that he (peace be upon him) is free of what was falsely attributed to him, whether by excess or by deficiency.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made﴾ and so on is a concluding statement (tadhyil) on the aspect of its indication of power, and that heedlessness comes from failing to reflect. It also contains an implicit rebuke (tadmin) of those who took the angels as gods, just as Jesus, peace be upon them, was taken. That is, had We willed, by Our power over wondrous affairs and marvellous natures, We would have made, by way of procreation (tawallud), and its outcome is "We would have procreated," ﴿from among you﴾, O men, ﴿angels﴾, just as We procreated Jesus without a father, ﴿in the earth, succeeding﴾, meaning they would succeed you on the earth as your children succeed you, or they would become a successor and offspring for you. This is so that Our distinction through overwhelming power is known, and so that it is known that angels are possible beings who are created by procreation as they are created by origination (ibda'). Then from where do they have the right to divinity and to being attributed to Him, glory be to Him, by sonship?

It has also been allowed that the meaning of "We would have made" is "We would have transformed some of you into angels," so that "min" is either for the beginning or for partition, and "angels" is a second object or a circumstantial accusative (hal). It has been said that "min" is for substitution (badal), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ and in the verse:

*"And he had not tasted, of the herbs, the pistachio."*

That is, had We willed, We would have made angels in your place, who would be in your stead after you were removed. The speech of Qatada and Mujahid points to this. The purpose is to show the completeness of His power, exalted is He, not the threat of annihilation, even though it is included, for that is not suited to the context. It has been said that there is no barrier to intending both together. Yes, many of the grammarians do not affirm that "min" carries the meaning of substitution, and they interpret what occurs that seems to imply it. The more evident is what was established first.

Al-Allama al-Tibi, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He is only a servant﴾ and so on is an answer to the disputation of the disbelievers in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship﴾ and so on. He stated that their argument is false, because (peace be upon him) was not included in that explicit text, since the address is to you, O polytheists, and you are the ones addressed by it. The intended meaning of "what you worship" is the idols which you carve with your hands. As for Jesus, peace be upon him, he is only a noble servant, favoured with prophethood, of exalted rank and renown among the Children of Israel, like a proverb in circulation. So how does he enter into our saying: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾? Then there is no objection against us in making one people fit for the Fire and others fit for Paradise, since if We willed, We would have made from among you and from your own selves, O disbelievers, angels, that is, noble servants, rightly guided, and bound for Paradise. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾. [End of al-Tibi's words.]

Based on what we have mentioned, the discourse concerning refutation is complete at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿contentious﴾, and what follows is for what you have heard before. This is more subtle and more fitting than what he mentioned. Indeed, what he indicated, that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had We willed﴾ and so on is for negating objection, is nothing.

It is narrated that Ibn al-Zib'ara said to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), when he heard His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾: "Is this for us and our gods, or for all the nations?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is for you, your gods, and all the nations." He said: "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Do not the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Jews worship 'Uzayr, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels? If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them." So they rejoiced and laughed, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), was silent. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed those for whom the good has preceded from Us﴾ and the verse. Or this verse was revealed. Some of them denied the silence, and mentioned that when Ibn al-Zib'ara said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "I have defeated you," the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), replied to him: "How ignorant you are of the language of your people! Did you not understand that 'ma' is for what does not reason?"

Muhyi al-Sunna in al-Ma'alim narrated that Ibn al-Zib'ara said to him, peace be upon him: "You said: 'Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell'?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do not the Jews worship 'Uzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?" Then the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), said: "Rather, they worship the Devil." Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed those for whom the good has preceded from Us﴾. This is more established than the report before it. The report before it, about Ibn al-Zib'ara's question, "Is this for us?" and so on, and his saying, peace be upon him: "It is for you" and so on, has been criticised as not authentic.

Whoever affirmed it mentioned that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), did not answer when asked about the particular and the general, with the particular, acting in accordance with what the word "ma" requires. For the exclusion of those specified from the ruling at the time of disputation, and they were permitted in their worship in general, so he generalised it, peace be upon him, to all. But not by way of the literal wording of the text, rather by way of implication (dalala), with the common ground being the sharing of being worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He. Then he made clear that they are far from being their objects of worship, by what came in the report of Muhyi al-Sunna, from his saying, peace be upon him: "Rather, they worship the Devil," as the saying of the Exalted attests: ﴿Glory be to You, You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ and the verse. What benefits you to remember has already been mentioned, so remember.

In al-Durr al-Manthur: Imam Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), said to the Quraysh: "There is no one worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He, in whom there is good." They said: "Do you not claim that Jesus was a prophet and a servant of Allah's servants, righteous? If you are truthful, then he is like our gods." So Allah, glory be to Him, revealed: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example﴾ and so on. The discourse concerning the verses according to this report is known from what has preceded with slight attention.

It has been said that when the polytheists heard His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust﴾, they said: "We are better guided than the Christians, for they worshipped a human being, and we worship the angels." So it was revealed. The example is what is in His saying: ﴿Indeed the likeness of Jesus﴾ and the verse, and the one who cites the example is Allah, exalted is His station. That is, when Allah, glory be to Him, made clear his wondrous state, your people took it as a means to promote the falsehood they are in, saying that although he was a created human being, he was worshipped; so we are better guided, since we worship angels, who are purified and honoured by Him. This is what they meant by their saying: ﴿Are our gods better, or he?﴾ Allah, exalted is He, refuted that, by saying that it is a comparison of falsehood with falsehood, and that they, in taking as god the favoured servant, are as much in error as you in taking the angels, who are honoured servants. Then the Exalted said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made from among you﴾, as proof that the angels, peace be upon them, are created like him, and that He, glory be to Him, is able to do what is more wondrous than the creation of Jesus, peace be upon him, and that there is no difference in that between what is created by procreation and what is created by origination. So neither of the two modes is suitable for divinity.

In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, when the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed the likeness of Jesus﴾ and the verse was revealed, the Quraysh said: "Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), intends by mentioning Jesus, peace be upon him, nothing but that we worship him as the Christians worshipped Jesus."

The meaning of yasiddun is yaḍijjun and yadjarun (they clamour and become vexed). The pronoun in "am" (or) refers to our Prophet, peace be upon him. Their purpose in weighing him against their gods was mockery of him, peace be upon him. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had We willed﴾ and so on is a rejection and refutation of their fabrication against him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), by making clear that Jesus, peace be upon him, in reality and in what was revealed to the Messenger, peace be upon him, is nothing but a favoured servant, as mentioned. So how would he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ), be pleased with being worshipped, or how could one imagine his being pleased with being worshipped himself? Then He, may His majesty be great, made clear that the likeness of Jesus is no novelty among the power of Allah, exalted is He, and that He is able to do something more wondrous than it, and more wondrous, while also alerting to the fall of the angels, peace be upon them, too, from the rank of being worshipped, by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Had We willed﴾ and so on. In this there is the point that the indication of that meaning is not clear. Likewise is the return of the pronoun to our Prophet, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿or he?﴾, together with its return to Jesus in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He is only a servant﴾. In this there is a disruption of the composition from which the inimitable Book must be preserved. And it can hardly be accepted that the second pronoun refers to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ). Perhaps the report about the event is not authentic. It has also been allowed that their intention was to disclaim what was denounced against them, namely their saying that the angels, peace be upon them, are daughters of Allah, glory be to Him, and their worship of them, as if they said: "We have not said a novel saying, nor done an objectionable deed. For the Christians made the Messiah the son of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, so we are superior to them in speech and deed, since we attribute to Him, exalted is He, the angels, peace be upon them, while they attributed to Him mere human beings." And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had We willed﴾ and so on is upon it, as in the second aspect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 43, verse 61:

﴿And indeed, it﴾, i.e., ʿIsā (Jesus), peace be upon him, ﴿is a sign (ʿilm) of the Hour﴾. That is, his descent is one of its signs (ashrāṭ), or his birth without a father, or his raising the dead is proof of the possibility of the Resurrection, which is the greatest of the matters that the disbelievers deny concerning the Hour. In any case, "the knowledge of the Hour" is a figurative usage (*majāz*) for that by which it is known, and the expression is used for emphasis.

Ubayy read (لَذِكْرٌ) (*ladhikrun*, "a reminder"), and this too is figurative in the same way.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah, Abū Mālik al-Ghifārī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mālik ibn Dīnār, al-Aʿmash, and al-Kalbī read (لَعَلَمٌ) (*la-ʿalamun*) with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and the lām, meaning "a sign" (*ʿalāmah*). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said so. Abū Naṣrah also read it this way.

ʿIkrimah, and Abū Naṣrah according to Ibn Khālawayh, read (لالعَلَمُ) (*la-l-ʿalamu*), definite, with two fatḥahs. The restriction (*ḥaṣr*) here is relative (*iḍāfī*). It is said that it is based on the consideration that he is the greatest of the signs. The traditions have indeed spoken of his descent, peace be upon him. Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Tirmidhī, Abū Dāwūd, and Ibn Mājah narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The son of Mary will certainly descend as a just judge. He will break the cross, kill the swine, abolish the jizyah, and the she-camels will be left unused so that no one will ride them. Rancour and enmity and envy will be removed, and he will call people to wealth, but no one will accept it."

In another narration: "He is descending. When you see him, recognize him: he is a man of medium height, inclining to redness and whiteness, descending between two garments dyed with saffron, as if his head is dripping, though no moisture has touched it. He will fight the people for Islam." In it also: "He will destroy the Messiah, the Dajjal (Antichrist)."

In another narration he said: "How will you be when the son of Mary descends among you and your Imam is from among you?" In another narration: "And he will lead you from among you." Ibn Abī Dhi'b said: "Do you know what 'he will lead you from among you' means?" He said: "Tell me." He said: "He will lead you by the Book of your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and the Sunnah of your Prophet (ﷺ)."

The well-known view is that he descends in Damascus while the people are in the Subh (dawn) prayer. The Imam, who is al-Mahdī (the guided one), then steps back, and ʿIsā, peace be upon him, moves him forward and prays behind him, saying: "It was established for you (to lead)."

It is also said that rather he advances and leads the people in prayer. Most scholars hold that he follows al-Mahdī in that prayer, to preclude the assumption that his descent abrogates (*naskh*) the law. As for other prayers, he leads the people himself, because he is the more excellent, but the Shīʿah (Shiites) reject this.

In some narrations, he, peace be upon him, descends at a pass (*thaniyyah*) called Afīq, with a fā' and a qāf, in the pattern of Amīr. Here it is a place in the noble Jerusalem itself. He remains on earth, according to a narration from Ibn ʿAbbās, for forty years, and in another narration for seven years. It is said that the forty years are the period of his stay before being raised and after (his return). Then he dies and is buried in the noble Prophetic chamber (*ḥujrah*). The full discussion is in *al-Buḥūr al-Zākhirah* by al-Safārīnī.

From al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and Ibn Jubayr it is narrated that the pronoun in ﴿And indeed, it﴾ refers to the Qur'an, because it contains the announcement of the Hour. So they made it the very knowledge, also for emphasis. This view is considered weak, because the Qur'an has not been mentioned here, and that interpretation does not fit the context. Another group said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), for he (ﷺ) said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two (fingers)." But this is far-fetched.

It seems these people also take the pronouns in ﴿or is he﴾ and ﴿if he is not﴾ to refer to him (ﷺ) as well, and that is, as you see, (far-fetched). ﴿So do not doubt it﴾, i.e., do not be in doubt about its occurrence. ﴿And follow Me﴾, i.e., follow My guidance, or My law (*sharʿī*), or My Messenger. It is also said that this is the statement of the Messenger (ﷺ), commanded by the Mighty and Majestic, so it has the implied speech "and say: follow me." ﴿This﴾, i.e., what I call you to, or the Qur'an, if the pronoun in "it" refers to it, ﴿is a straight path﴾ leading to the truth.

[Page 96]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 62:

﴿And let not Satan avert you (from following me). Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ That is, (he is) manifest in enmity, or one who displays it, since he caused your father to be expelled from the Garden and exposed you to tribulation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 63:

﴿And when Jesus came with the clear proofs﴾, that is, with the manifest matters, which are the miracles, or the verses of the Injil (Gospel), or the sacred laws; and there is no barrier to intending all of them. ﴿He said﴾ to the Children of Israel: ﴿Indeed I have come to you with wisdom﴾, that is, the Injil, as al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi said. Al-Suddi said: with prophethood; and in another report from him: it is matters which reason judges. Abu Hayyan said: that is, with what the divine wisdom requires of the laws. Al-Dahhak said: that is, with admonition. ﴿And to make clear to you﴾ is connected to an omitted element, that is, "and I have come to make clear to you." He did not leave out the conjunction so that it would attach to what precedes it, in order to indicate concern with the reason, since it is made as though it were an independent statement. In al-Irshad it says: it is a conjunction upon an omitted element indicated by the coming with wisdom, as if it were said: "I have come to you with wisdom, to teach you it and to make clear to you ﴿some of that about which you differ﴾", and that is the matter of religious obligations and what relates to legal responsibility, not the matters which they were not commanded to know, such as the manner of the arrangement of the spheres and the causes of the differing shapes of the moon, for example; the prophets, peace be upon them, were not sent to clarify what is disputed concerning such things. Similar to these is what relates to worldly affairs, such as the manner of cultivation and what improves or spoils crops, for example; the prophets, peace be upon them, were not sent to clarify these either, as the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the matter of pollinating the palm trees indicates: «You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life».

It is also permitted that by this "some" is meant some of the matters of religion that are binding, and by "clarify" is meant clarification in detail; and it is not possible to clarify all of them in detail, and some of them are left to ijtihad (independent reasoning). Abu Ubayda said: the intended meaning is some of what was forbidden to them, and peace be upon him made lawful for them the flesh of camels, the fat of every animal, and the hunting of fish on the Sabbath day. Mujahid said: some of what they differ about, from the alteration of the Torah. Qatadah said: to make clear to you the disagreement of those who split into factions concerning his matter, peace be upon him. ﴿So fear Allah﴾ regarding my opposition, ﴿and obey me﴾ in what I convey to you from Him, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.﴾ This is an explanation of that which He commanded them to obey, namely the belief in tawhid (the oneness of God) and worship through the sacred laws (shara'i') ﴿This﴾, that is, this tawhid and worship through the sacred laws, ﴿is a straight path﴾ whose traveler does not go astray. It may be part of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, or a resumption (isti'naf) from Allah, the Exalted, affirming the statement of Jesus, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 65:

﴿Then the factions differed﴾ (al-ahzab), meaning the groups that formed parties ﴿among themselves﴾, that is, among those to whom he was sent and whom he addressed with what he addressed them with, namely the Jews and the Christians, who were the community of his call, peace be upon him. It was also said: the intended meaning is the Christians, who were the community of his response, peace be upon him. They split into sects: the Melkite (Malkaniyya), the Nestorian (Nasturiyya), and the Jacobite (Ya'qubiyya).

﴿So woe to those who did wrong﴾ from among those who differed, and they are those who did not say that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger, ﴿from the punishment of a painful day﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection. "Painful" (alim) is an attribute of the punishment, or of the day by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi).

The pronoun in ﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ refers to the Quraysh. ﴿أنْ تَأْتِيَهم﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿السّاعَةَ﴾, and the exception is an exceptive construction with the stated object omitted (al-istithna' al-mufarragh). It is also permissible to make ﴿إلّا﴾ mean ﴿غَيْرِ﴾ ("other than"), with the interrogative expressing denial. ﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ means ﴿يَنْتَظِرُونَ﴾ ("await"), so the sense is: they await nothing but the Hour coming upon them suddenly while they are heedless of it. In this there is a mockery of them, since the coming of the Hour is presented as something awaited that must certainly occur.

Since suddenness (al-fajah) and awareness (al-shu'ur) can coexist, it was necessary to qualify this with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ ("while they are unaware"), because the first does not dispense with the second, and so there is no rectification (istidrak) here. It has been said that ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ may be taken to affirm something, because the statement comes in the form of a denial, as if it were said: "Do they suppose that it will come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?" That is, it will not be so; rather it will come upon them while they are alert. In this there is what there is.

It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ refers to those who did wrong, and it has been said that it refers to people in general. This is reinforced by what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will be established while two men are milking a ewe and two men are folding a garment," then he (ﷺ) recited: ﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إلا السّاعَةَ أنْ تَأْتِيَهم بَغْتَةً وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾.

The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing. The adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) is connected to "enemies" (*'aduww*), and the intervening separation (*al-fasl*) does not harm that connection. The meaning is that loves will be severed on the Day when the Hour comes upon them, and only the love of the God-fearing (*al-muttaqin*) will remain, for they are those who are friends for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because they see the reward of loving one another for the sake of Allah, exalted. The severance is described this way because a close friend, insofar as he is a close friend, cannot become an enemy.

It was said: the meaning is that the friendship of close friends will be cut off that day, except for those who avoided evil companions. The difference between the two views is that the God-fearing in the first is one who loves his companion for Allah, so he guards against love being tainted by a non-divine motive; in the second, he is one who has avoided the companionship of evildoers.

The exception (*istithna'*) in both views is connected (*muttasil*). It is permissible that "that day" be connected to "close friends," meaning in this world, and that the complement of "enemies" be understood as implied, i.e., in the Hereafter. It was said that the verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it.

Quran 43:68: "O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve."

This is a quotation recounting what will be called out to the mutually loving (al-mutahabbun) for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, on that Day. It is therefore in the sense of an implied "saying" (taqdir qawl), i.e., "it will be said to them: O My servants..." etc., or "I will say to them," on the basis that the one calling out is Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, as an honour to them.

It is related from al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman that when people are resurrected, none of them is without alarm, and a caller calls out: "O servants..." etc., and all the people hope for it, and so they follow it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 69:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾ — "then the disbelievers will despair of them." "O My servants" is general but specified, either by the preceding verse or by the following one, and the first is more in accord with it in many respects.

The relative clause (al-mawsul) is either an attribute (sifah) of the vocative (al-munada), or a substitute (badal), or an object of an implied verb, i.e., "I praise" or the like. The clause ﴿and were Muslims﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿believed﴾, with qad implied or without it. Its coordination (ataf) to the relative clause has also been permitted. The circumstantial reading is preferred, because the discourse with it is more eloquent, since the intended sense of "submission" (al-Islam) here is compliance (al-infiyad) and sincerity (al-ikhlas), so that mentioning it after faith conveys that, after their engagement with it in the past, their connection to the time of faith continues, and "was" (kana) also indicates continuity. From here comes the emphasis and the greater eloquence, unlike coordination. The same applies to the single-word circumstantial (al-hal al-mufradah), by saying: "Those who believed in Our signs, sincerely." 

Many of the Seven Readers read "O My servants" (ya ibadi) with the ya, according to the original form, while elision is very common and widespread; and Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it thus. Ibn Muhaysin read "No fear" (la khawfun) with a raised vowel without tanwin, and al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa, Ibn Ya'mur and Ya'qub read it with a fatha without tanwin.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 70:**

﴿Enter the Garden, you and your spouses﴾: your wives, the believing women. The annexation (*idafah*, the possessive or genitive construction) indicates complete exclusivity (*ikhtisas al-tamm*), so whoever among them did not believe is excluded. ﴿You will be delighted﴾: you will be made to rejoice with a joy whose *hibar* (its visible trace, meaning its effect) appears as radiance (*nadrah*) and beauty upon your faces, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾. Or it means: you will be adorned, from *al-habr*, pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the *ha'*, which is adornment and good appearance. In meaning this is identical with what precedes it, and the difference lies in the root from which it is derived. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., you will be honored with an honoring carried to an extreme. *Al-habrah* with a fatha is the intensification of the act described as beautiful, and from it comes *ikram* (honoring). So in origin the word is general, and here some of its instances are intended.

﴿They will be circulated among them﴾ after their entry into Paradise, wherever they are commanded, ﴿with platters of gold and cups﴾ likewise. The ṣiḥāf (platters) is the plural of ṣaḥfah, which is said to be like a qaṣʿah (large bowl). It is also said that the greatest of the vessels for eating is the jafnah, then the qaṣʿah, then the ṣaḥfah, then the kaylah.

The akwāb (cups) is the plural of kūb, which is a kūz (jug) without a handle. This is the meaning of Mujahid's saying "without an ear" (lā udhuna lah). According to what is narrated from Qatadah, it is [a vessel] without a spout, unlike the ibrīq (ewer), and he said: "We have been told that its head is rounded." Since vessels for food are generally more numerous than vessels for drink, the first [term] is in the plural of abundance (jam' kathrah) and the second in the plural of paucity (jam' qillah). Reports concerning the abundance of platters are indeed numerous. Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Ṣifat al-Jannah, and al-Ṭabarani in al-Awsat, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, reported from Anas who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The lowest of the people of Paradise in rank is the one for whom ten thousand servants stand at his head, each holding in his hand two platters, one of gold and the other of silver; in each one there is a color not found in the other. He eats from the last of them as he eats from the first, and he finds in the last of them the same goodness and pleasure as he finds in the first. Then that becomes like the sweat of the strongly scented musk. They do not urinate, nor defecate, nor blow their noses, [but are] brothers, upon couches, facing one another.'" And in a ḥadīth narrated by ʿIkrimah: "The one with the lowest station and the lowest rank among the people of Paradise is a man after whom no one else will enter. His sight will be extended to a distance of a year's journey, [and he will be in] palaces of gold and tents of pearls, in which there is no span of space except that it is populated. He will be served every morning and evening with seventy thousand platters, in each platter a color not found in the other; his desire at the last of them is like his desire at the first. Even if all the people of the earth descended upon him, it would suffice them from what he has been given, and that would not diminish anything of what he has been given." Ibn Abi Shaybah also narrated this number from Kaʿb. And if that is the case for the lowest, then what do you think of the highest? May Allah grant us what befits His generosity and His munificence.

Abu al-Harith, from al-Kisa'i, as mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh, inclined [the alif of] "bi-ṣiḥāfin" [toward ē-sound]. ﴿And therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise, ﴿is what the souls desire﴾ of the various kinds of delights, ﴿and what the eyes find delight in﴾, i.e., they take pleasure in it and are gladdened by beholding it. The mention of this comprehensive [category], which includes every pleasure and bliss, after mention of the circulating [of vessels] among them with vessels of gold, which is a part of luxury and affluence, is a generalization after a specification, just as the mention of the delight of the eye, which is the spy of the soul, after the desire of the soul, is a specification after a generalization. Some of the eminent scholars said: God's words "They will be circulated among them with platters" indicate foods, and "and cups" indicate drinks. It is not far-fetched that His words "And therein is what the souls desire" be understood as referring to marriage, clothing, and what is connected to them, so that all the desirable pleasures of the soul are complete. Then the greatest pleasure remains, which is gazing upon the face of Allah, the Generous, and so it is alluded to by His words "and what the eyes find delight in." For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, as narrated by al-Nasa'i from Anas: "Perfume and women have been made beloved to me, and the coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer."

Qays ibn Mulawwah said:
"I had resolved to kill her out of my love for her, so that she would be my adversary on the Gathering [Day],
Until our standing upon the Ṣirāt is prolonged, and my eye is delighted by the delightful sight."

This agrees with the saying of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "How far apart is what the souls desire from what the eyes find delight in! For all that is in Paradise of bliss and desires, compared to what the eyes find delight in, is like a finger dipped into the sea, because the desires of Paradise have a limit and an end, being created, whereas no eye is delighted in the Abode of Permanence except by gazing upon the Everlasting, Majestic and Exalted, and there is no limit to that, nor description, nor end." End of quote. From what has been mentioned it is known that the meaning, on the reading "and therein is what the eyes find delight in," is as follows; and al-Zamakhshari built his statement on this: "This is a restriction of the kinds of blessings, for they are either desired in the hearts or delighted in by the eyes." Al-Kashshaf (or rather its commentator) criticized him, saying: "There is a problem with it, because it is refuted by the delights of the other five senses. If it is said that these belong to the first category, we say: the delight of the eye is likewise. Rather, the correct view is that it was mentioned to magnify its bliss, by [pointing to] something in which the heart and the eye agree, and which is for them the ultimate in what is beloved, because the eye is the forerunner of the heart." This is a statement that in the second clause there is no consideration of a separate relative pronoun; rather it and the clause before it are two relative clauses of one antecedent, which is the one mentioned. What preceded is what the majority of scholars' words imply, and omitting the relative pronoun in such a context is common. There is no barrier to including the gazing upon the face of the Generous Allah within "what the eyes find delight in," according to what we mentioned at first. The "al-" in "al-anfus" and "al-a'yun" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), according to what has been said, and there is no difference between the plural of paucity and the plural of abundance.

Perhaps someone who says that the comprehensiveness of the singular is more inclusive than that of the plural, and who distinguishes between the two plurals at the beginning and end, would say that the comprehensiveness of the plural of paucity is more inclusive than that of the plural of abundance. It was also said that the "al-" is for prior reference (ʿahd), and it was said that it is a substitute for the genitive complement, i.e., "what their souls desire and their eyes find delight in." The plural of nafs and of ʿayn (in the sense of seeing eye) in the form afʿul is more common in their speech than their plural in other forms; indeed, in the noble Qur'an, the plural of bāṣirah (seeing eye) occurs only in that form. How fitting this plural is here because of the mention of "the intimate friends" (al-akhilla')! Understanding what the souls desire as referring to marriage, clothing, and what is connected to them is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Also in the reports there is what is apparent in generality. Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Buraydah who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Are there horses in Paradise? For they please me.' He said: 'If you wish that, you will be brought a horse of red ruby which will fly you about in Paradise wherever you wish.' Then another man said to him: 'Camels please me; are there camels in Paradise?' He said: 'O servant of Allah, if you are admitted into Paradise, there will be for you therein what your soul desires and your eye finds delight in.'"

A similar [report] was also narrated from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: "It is more authentic than the first," and similar [reports] came in other narrations, so the criticism of its chain's weakness does not harm it. Nor does it pose a problem for the generality that sodomy, for example, does not occur in Paradise, because what is not fitting to be there is not desired. Rather, it was said specifically of sodomy that sound souls do not desire it in this world.

People differed as to whether pregnancy occurs in Paradise or not. Some went to the first view: al-Imam Ahmad, Hannad, al-Darimi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, children are the coolness of the eye and the completion of joy; will children be born to the people of Paradise?' He, upon whom be prayer and peace, said: 'When a believer desires a child in Paradise, its pregnancy, its birth, and its growth to maturity will occur in an hour, as he desires.'"

Ṭawus, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Mujahid, ʿAṭāʾ, and Ishaq ibn Ibrahim went to the second view. It is narrated from Abu Razin al-ʿUqayli, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The people of Paradise will not have children." In the long ḥadīth of Laqit, narrated by ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad, Abu Bakr ibn ʿAmr, Abu Ahmad Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban, Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Mandah, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and a group of the ḥuffāẓ (memorizers of ḥadīth), which the imams received with acceptance, Ibn Mandah said about it: "None denies this ḥadīth except one who is obstinate, ignorant, or opposed to the Book and the Sunnah." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we have wives therein—meaning Paradise—and will some of them be righteous?" He said: "The righteous women are for the righteous men; you will enjoy them and they will enjoy you, like your pleasures in this world, except that there will be no procreation."

Mujahid and ʿAṭāʾ said regarding the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾, i.e., purified from children, menstruation, excrement, urine, and the like. Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, in the ḥadīth of Abu Sa'id mentioned earlier, said: its meaning is: when the believer desires a child in Paradise, its pregnancy, birth, and growth occur in an hour as he desires, but he does not desire [it]. This was criticized on the grounds that "idhā" is for what is certain to occur, and if what was mentioned were intended, it would have said "law ishtaha" (if he were to desire). In Ḥādī al-Arwāḥ, the isnad of the ḥadīth of Abu Sa'id is said to be according to the condition of the sound ones, its narrators being those who may be relied upon in it, but it is extremely strange. Al-Safarini said in al-Buhur al-Zakhirah: "The best of the chains of the ḥadīth of Abu Sa'id is the chain of al-Tirmidhi," and he ruled it strange, and that it is not known except from the ḥadīth of Abu al-Siddiq al-Naji. Its wording is disturbed: sometimes it is reported as "when he desires a child," sometimes "that he desires a child," and sometimes "that a man is born to him." "Idhā" may be used merely for general conditional meaning, which is broader than what is certain and other [than it]. The view of no birth was preferred for ten reasons mentioned therein. I myself choose the view of birth, as the ḥadīth of Abu Sa'id states. Al-Ustadh Abu Sahl said of it, as transmitted by al-Hakim: "None denies it except the people of deviation," and it has more than one chain. The formation of a child in Paradise is not in the known manner of this world, but it is formed as the ḥadīth states, and when it is so, it is not unlikely that it is formed from a breeze that comes out at the time of intercourse. It is claimed that a child is created only from semen, so where there is no semen in Paradise, as the reports say, there is no creation; this is a limitation upon [divine] power. This does not contradict the ḥadīth of Laqit, because what is meant there is the negation of procreation as known in this world, as the phrase "except that there is no procreation" after his words, upon whom be prayer and peace, "like your pleasures in this world," indicates. Something similar is said regarding the ḥadīth of Abu Razin, to reconcile the reports. Moreover, procreation is not continuous; rather it follows desire, and its continuation is not necessary. The claim that if it continued, it would necessitate the existence of endless individuals, and if it ceased, it would necessitate the cessation of a kind of pleasure of the people of Paradise, is nothing. As for what is claimed: it is firmly established in the authentic [reports] that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There will remain in Paradise a surplus, and Allah will create for it a creation to settle them therein," and if there were procreation in Paradise, the surplus would be for their children who are constantly with them, that is not granted, since one may say: whoever desires a child desires that it be with him in his dwelling. The claim that procreation in this world is for the wisdom of preserving the species, and that the species remains in Paradise without procreation, so it would be pointless, is answered by saying: what prevents there being, for pleasure and the like, something like eating and drinking, which in this world serve one purpose and in Paradise serve another? In sum, what has been mentioned among the aspects for preferring non-procreation is not hidden in its weakness from one who has sound understanding.

Many of the Seven and others read "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus wa-taladdhu al-aʿyun" with the pronoun referring to "mā" omitted from both coordinated clauses. In the Codex of ʿAbd Allah, it reads "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus wa-taladdhu-hu al-aʿyun" with the pronoun in both. The reading with the pronoun in the first clause, but not the second, belongs to Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥafṣ. ﴿And you therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise. It was also said: in the delights.

the (not fully) "Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 71 (part 2 of 2)"

Translation of the passage:

...understood from what preceded, and it is, as you see, ﴿abiding forever﴾: remaining eternally, forever and ever. The sentence falls within the scope of the address and serves as an emphasis of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No fear shall be upon you﴾. They were addressed with this in order to complete the blessing and perfect the joy, for every bliss that is transient necessitates the burden of guarding it and fear of its passing, and it leads to regret in later states. And how well the poet said, may God Most High reward him:

"When you reflect, a passing hardship
is better for a man than a passing bliss."

And it is related from al-Nasrabadhi that if their abiding was for the desire of the souls and the pleasure of the eyes, then annihilation is better than that; but if it was for the annihilation of attributes and for being characterized by the attributes of the Truth, and for abiding therein upon the couches of contentment and contemplation, then "you, then, are you" (i.e., you remain as you are). You know that what he mentioned enters the general meaning of what preceded by way of first entry. Some of them mentioned here that the address here is from the rhetorical device of al-iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and that it is for honor.

Al-Tibi said: Taste, along with your upright disposition, the meaning of the address, the iltifat, and the fronting of the adverbial phrase in ﴿and you therein abide forever﴾, so that you may stand upon what description cannot encompass.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 72:

﴿Such is the Garden﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject) and *khabar* (predicate). His statement, exalted is He, ﴿which you have been made to inherit﴾ is a *sifah* (qualifying adjective) of "the Garden." His statement, glorified is He, ﴿for what you used to do﴾ is related to *ʾūrithtumūhā* (you have been made to inherit it). It has also been said that ﴿Such is the Garden﴾ is a *mubtada'* and *sifah*, and ﴿which you have been made to inherit﴾ is the *khabar*, with the prepositional phrase after it related to it. It has also been said that ﴿such﴾ is a *mubtada'*, "the Garden" is its *sifah*, ﴿which you have been made to inherit﴾ is a *sifah* of "the Garden," and ﴿for what you used to do﴾ is related to an elided element, which is the *khabar*.

According to the first reading, the demonstrative refers to the Garden mentioned in His statement, ﴿Enter the Garden﴾. According to the last two readings, it refers to the Garden that is described as a qualifier, as has been said. The *bā'* (ب) here is causal (*sababiyyah*) or indicates exchange (*muqābalah*). What they deserved has been likened to the lasting bliss of the Garden that is theirs because of their good deeds, to what a person leaves to his heir of property and provisions. This necessarily makes their own deeds resemble the one who bequeaths, in the form of an active participle. So the word "inheritance" was borrowed for what they deserved, and then *ʾūrithtumūhā* was derived from it. Thus there is a *isti'ārah tab'iyyah* (verbal metaphor based on a derived form). Some have said the metaphor is *tamthīliyyah* (an extended metaphorical image).

It is also permissible that it be *makniyyah* (implicit metaphor). It has also been said that "inheritance" is a *majāz mursal* (a metonymic figurative usage) meaning attainment and receiving. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no one but that he has a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in Hell. The disbeliever inherits the believer's dwelling in Hell, and the believer inherits the disbeliever's dwelling in Paradise." That is the meaning of His statement: ﴿Such is the Garden which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do﴾. The speech also contains a figurative element according to this as well. In any case, the causal relation of deeds to the inheriting and attaining of the Garden is only by the grace of Allah and His mercy, mighty and majestic is He. What is meant by the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds alone," is that the deed causing entry into Paradise is not on its own and by complete causation; so there is no contradiction.

Hannad and Abd ibn Humayd in *al-Zuhd* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "You will cross the *Sirat* (bridge) by the pardon of Allah, the Exalted, you will enter Paradise by the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, and you will divide the dwellings by your deeds. So reflect." It has also been read as (ورِثْتُمُوها) *wirthtumūhā*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 73:

﴿For you therein is abundant fruit⁠﴾ — abundant according to kinds and varieties, not merely according to individual pieces. ﴿From it you eat⁠﴾ — meaning you eat only some of it, while its stems remain intact on its trees. Thus the trees are always adorned with fruit and laden with it; no tree is seen bare of its fruit as in this world. There is a hadith: "No man in Paradise plucks from its fruit except that there grows in its place two like it." So "min" (from) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), though it has been permitted that it be initial (ibtida'iyyah). The fronting [of the object] is for exclusive restriction in relation to others (al-hasr al-idafi). It has also been said that it is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fasilah).

Perhaps the repeated mention of foods in the Mighty Qur'an, although they are as nothing compared with the rest of the blessings of Paradise, is because most of its addressees in this world suffered hardship and want; so it is a consolation to them. It has also been said that this is because most of those addressed were common people, whose outlook was confined to eating and drinking. This has been criticised as not being complete. The Sufis have remarks on this which will come in other places, God willing, Mighty and Majestic is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 74:

﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾
Page 102
That is, those who are persistent in criminality, who are complete in it, and they are the disbelievers. It is as if it were said: Indeed, the disbelievers ﴿will abide in the punishment of Hell﴾. He strengthened the intention of this by making them the counterpart of the believers in the verses, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believed in Our verses﴾. Thus the verse does not indicate the eternal abiding (khulud) of the sinful believers, as the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij maintain. The fact that the verse does not address the ruling concerning them does not harm, on the basis that what is meant by ﴿those who believed﴾ is the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve﴾. As for the view that ﴿those who believed﴾ includes them, because the reason (al-'illah) is their faith and submission, its weakness is not hidden. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is related to ﴿abiding﴾, and ﴿abiding﴾ is the predicate of inna (khabar inna). It is also permitted that the adverbial phrase be the predicate, with ﴿abiding﴾ being its subject (fa'il) because it depends on the preceding word (li'timadihi).

"They will not be relieved of it" — that is, it will not be lightened for them, from "fatarat 'anhu al-humma" (the fever subsided, i.e., abated for a little while). The root, in whatever form it appears, indicates weakness in general.

"And they will be in it" — that is, in the torment. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read "fiha," meaning in Jahannam.

"Mublisun" — despairing, grieved because of the severity of the affliction. Al-Raghib said: al-iblas is the grief that overtakes a person from the severity of the affliction, and from it, it is said, Iblis is derived.

Since the one who is mublis often remains silent and forgets what concerns him, it is said: "Ublisa fulan" when a person falls silent and his argument is cut off. The meaning of iblas is explained here as silence and the cutting off of argument.

﴿And We did not wrong them, but they themselves were the wrongdoers.﴾ That is, because of the evil of their own choice.

Here, *humu* (هُمُ) is a *ḍamīr faṣl* (separating pronoun, a pronoun placed between two parts of a sentence), and it conveys restriction (*takhṣīṣ*).

ʿAbdullāh and Abū Zayd read *al-ẓālimūna* (الظّالِمُونَ) in the nominative, taking *hum* as the *mubtadaʾ* (subject) with what follows as its *khabar* (predicate). Abū ʿUmar al-Jirmī mentioned that the dialect of Tamīm is to treat what is a separating pronoun for others as a *mubtadaʾ*, and they put the word following it in the nominative as the *khabar*. Abū Zayd said: "I heard them reading *taǧidūhu ʿinda Allāhi huwa khayrun wa-aʿẓamu* (تَجِدُوهُ عِنْدَ اَللَّهِ هو خَيْرٌ وأعْظَمُ), with *khayrun* and *aʿẓamu* in the nominative."

Qays ibn Dhurayḥ said:

*You long for Layla though you have left her,*
*and you were, in company, the one more able to be with her.*

Sībawayh said: "It has reached us that Ruʾba used to say: *aẓunnu Zaydan huwa khayrun minka* (أظُنُّ زَيْدًا هو خَيْرٌ مِنكَ), meaning with the nominative."

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** (Alusi) on surah 43, verse 77:

﴿They will call out﴾, that is, from the intensity of the punishment.

It is reported in some narrations that hunger will be inflicted on the people of the Fire until it equals the torment they are in. They will say, "Call Malik," and so they will call, ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us﴾, that is, let Him cause us to die, since one who is decreed upon is made to die when He causes him to die. Their intent is: "Ask your Lord to decree an end for us so that we may find rest." Their referring to Him as "your Lord" (rather than "our Lord") is to urge Malik, not to deny. This does not contradict their despair (iblas) according to the first interpretation, because it is a cry and a wish for death out of extreme severity. As for the second interpretation, that they will not have the despair: although it is negated, the time of each state is different from the time of the other, since the periods of punishment are long and its eons extended. Their conditions therefore vary: they fall silent at times because despair overcomes them and they know there is no escape for them, not even through death, and at other times they cry out for help because of the intensity of what they suffer.

It has been objected that this does not suit the continuance of the nominal clause, namely "while they are in despair." It has also been said that "they will call out" is conjoined by "and" (wa), which does not require sequence. But it is not hidden that this clause is circumstantial (hali) and does not separate from eternal abiding.

Ali, may God ennoble his countenance, and Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Wathhab, and al-A'mash read ﴿Yā Māl﴾ with apocope (tarkhim, the clipping of the final letter of a vocative), according to the dialect of one who awaits (the speaker who keeps the clipped form in pause). Abu al-Sawwar read ﴿Yā Māl﴾ also with apocope, but according to the dialect of one who does not await.

Ibn Jinni said: There is a secret in apocope in this place. Because of the greatness of what they are in, their strength weakened and their souls were humbled, so abbreviation here was a necessity. By this the saying of Ibn Abbas may be answered, when this reading was related to him in the first dialect: "What has occupied the people of the Fire away from apocope!" He thereby indicated his rejection of it, for "mā" here expresses wonder, and it carries the sense of prevention. That is, they are in a state that occupies them from turning to apocope and from abandoning the call in the more common usage. The summary of the answer is that this apocope did not issue from them with the intention of varying speech and embellishing it, as in the verse:

*It revives the decayed bones, crumbling,*
*And the truth, O Mal, is other than what you describe.*

Rather it was due to incapacity and the narrowness of the scope for completing the word, as is observed in some who are in distress.

﴿He said﴾, that is, Malik, ﴿Indeed you will abide﴾, remaining in the punishment forever, with no escape from it for you by death or otherwise. This is despair and a blow upon them beyond what they are in. Nor does it harm this that he knows of their despair, if we hold that view.

Some eminent scholars mentioned that there is mockery in this, because he put "abiding" in the place of "eternity," and abiding suggests cessation, since, as al-Raghib said, it is steadfastness together with waiting. The aspect of mockery may also be the expression "abiding" (mākithūn), insofar as it suggests choice, and their answer comes with that after a period.

Ibn Abbas said: He answers them after a thousand years have passed. Nawf said: after a hundred. It was also said eighty, and it was said forty.
