Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 78:

﴿Indeed, We brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾ This is an address of reproach and rebuke from the side of God, Exalted is He, confirming the answer of Malik and explaining the reason for their staying (in the Fire). There is no obstacle to His, glorified is He, addressing the disbelievers in order to rebuke them. It has also been said that it is part of the speech of some of the angels, peace be upon them, and it is like when one of the servants of the king says to the subjects: "We informed you and we acted toward you." It has been said that it cannot be the speech of Malik, not because of the plural pronoun (which rules it out), but because it is not fitting for Malik to say it, since he has no service other than guarding the Fire.

In this there is a point for discussion. It has been said that the pronoun in (qala, "he said") refers to Him, Exalted is He, so that the whole is His speech, Mighty and Majestic is He. It has also been said that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, you will remain (forever)﴾ is the concluding state of the two groups, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, We brought you...﴾ and so on, is another statement addressed to the Quraysh. The intended meaning of "We brought you the truth" in this case is (in) this surah or the Qur'an. According to what preceded, "We brought you the truth" means in the world, and the truth is monotheism and the rest of what must be believed, and that (was done) by sending the messengers and revealing the books. ﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾, i.e., to whatever truth it was: they do not accept it and they shy away from it. The truth was interpreted in this way rather than as the known truth, whether the address is to the people of the Fire or to the Quraysh, because of the phrase ﴿most of you﴾, for the known truth is one that all of them are averse to and recoil from. It may be said: the apparent meaning is the known truth, and the word "most" was used because among the followers there are some who disbelieve by imitation. And it has been read: (laqad ji'natakum), "We have come to you."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they determined a matter?﴾ is a new (independent) statement, censuring the polytheists for the plotting they carried out against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The particle (am) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and what it implies is the meaning of (bal) (rather), for the transition from rebuking the people of the Fire to narrating the crime of these people. The interrogative hamza is for denial. If by "determining" (al-ibram) is meant the actual decreeing of a matter, then it denies its occurrence and its likelihood; and if by it is meant the decreeing in appearance, then it denies what has occurred and condemns it. That is: rather, the polytheists of Makkah have determined a matter of their scheming and deceit against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Then indeed We are determining⦆ Our plan in reality, not theirs; or, ﴿Then indeed We are determining Our plan against them⦈ in reality, just as they determined their plan in appearance, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they intend a scheme? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be ensnared.﴾ The verse alludes to what they did of plotting to kill him, peace and blessings be upon him, in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh), and to what came from Him, mighty and majestic, of their destruction.

It has also been said that it is part of the preceding statement, and the meaning is: Or have they determined, in rejecting the truth and turning it back, and did not limit themselves to disliking it? Then indeed We are determining a matter in requiting them. If that address is to the people of the Fire, then the determining of the matter in requiting them is their being eternally abiding in the Fire, being punished; and if it is an address to the Quraysh, then it is their abandonment and the Prophet's (ﷺ) victory over them. So it is as if it were said: Then indeed We are determining a matter in requiting them and manifesting your affair. In this there is an allusion that their determination does not benefit them, nor does it avail them anything. The shift from direct address in ﴿Or have they determined﴾ to the third person in (abramu, "they determined") on this reading is to indicate that this is worse than their disliking.

And this is supported by what was mentioned earlier, according to what has been said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 80:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret [talk] and their private consultation?﴾ This is because it indicates that what they had plotted was a matter they had concealed, which suits [the context of] scheming rather than denying the truth, since the disbelievers are openly [defiant] in that. By "secret" (sirr) is meant here inner discourse (hadith al-nafs), i.e., "Or do they think that We do not hear the inner discourse of their souls concerning that scheming?" ﴿And their private consultation﴾, i.e., their confidential conferring and conversing in secret.

Another group said: "The secret (sirr) is what they spoke to themselves or to others in a private place, and the private consultation (najwa) is what they said among themselves by way of confidential conferring." ﴿Yes [indeed]﴾, We hear both and are aware of them. ﴿And Our messengers﴾, who preserve their deeds for them, ﴿are with them﴾, constantly attending them, ﴿recording﴾, i.e., they record both of these, or they record everything that issues from them of deeds and words, of which the aforementioned is a part.

The present tense (al-mudari') denotes renewed continuity (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi). It, together with its subject, is a predicate (khabar); and (ladayhim) is a circumstantial phrase (hal), placed first for the sake of the rhyme (fasila), or it is also a predicate. The nominal sentence is either coordinated (ataf) with what "Yes" implies, or it is a circumstantial clause, i.e., "We hear that, while Our messengers are recording it." And if the meaning of "secret" is inner discourse, then the verse clearly indicates that the secret and the imagined speech are heard by Him, Exalted is He; and likewise it clearly indicates that the guardian angels record it just as they record their other outward words and deeds. It is not far-fetched that God Exalted might make them aware of it through one of the means of awareness, so that they record it.

As for those who restrict their scribes to matters other than those of the heart, they restrict "secret" to what is spoken to another in a private place. The apparent meaning is that their supposition was genuine, and it is not unlikely among ignorant disbelievers. Ibn Jarir related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: While three men were by the Ka'bah and its curtains, two Qurashis and a Thaqafi, or two Thaqafis and a Qurashi, one of them said: "Do you think God, Exalted, hears what we say?" Another said: "If you speak aloud, He hears; if you speak secretly, He does not hear." So the verse was revealed: ﴿Or do they think﴾, and so on.

It has also been said that their conduct, in their boldness toward falsehood and their lack of fear of God, Mighty and Majestic, was like the conduct of one who supposes that God, glory be to Him, does not hear his secret and his private consultation.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 81:**

﴿Say﴾, that is, to the disbelievers, to establish the truth and to alert them that your opposition to them, by not worshipping what they worship of the angels (peace be upon them), is not due to your hatred and enmity towards them or towards their objects of worship. Rather, it is due to your certainty that what they attribute to them, and on which they built their worship, is impossible, namely that they are the daughters of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ That is, [I would be the first to worship] that son. Here *kāna* is used in the sense of *ṣaḥḥa* (to be valid), as one says *mā kāna laka an taf'ala kadhā* ("it is not for you to do such-and-such"), and this is one of its usages. *Awwal* (first) is an elative (*af'al al-tafḍīl*), and the one it is compared to is those addressed. It is also permissible to consider it unrestricted, and the intention is to express desire and eagerness. What comes first to mind is the first interpretation.

The implication (*wajh al-mulāzama*) is that he, peace be upon him, is the most knowledgeable of people about the affairs of Allah, the Exalted, and about what is permissible for Him and what is not, and the most eager to observe His rights and what they require, including the glorifying of His son, glorified is He. For the right of a father over a person requires that person to glorify his son, since glorifying the son is glorifying the father. Thus the meaning is: if the Most Merciful had a son, and that were valid and established by a sound proof that you present and a clear argument by which you reason, then I am the first to glorify that son, and the first to submit to him and obey him, just as a man glorifies the son of a king because of the greatness of his father. This is a negation of the existence of a son for Him, glorified is He, in the most eloquent manner, through the demonstrative method (*al-ṭarīq al-burhānī*) and the theological approach (*al-madhhab al-kalāmī*). In reality, it is an exceptive conditional syllogism (*qiyās istithnā'ī*), in which the negation of the consequent, whose absence is evident, is used to infer the negation of the antecedent. The consequent is his, peace and blessings be upon him, worship of the son, and the antecedent is the existence of a son for Him, glorified is He. This is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there were in them [the heavens and the earth] gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾. However, *in* was used instead of *law* (if), to place what falls under its scope on the level of what is not definitively known to be non-existent, by way of leniency and loosening the reins for rebuke and silencing.

[Page 105]

In *al-Kashshāf* it is stated that there is hyperbole in the verse, in that it made the possible in itself, namely his worship, peace be upon him, of what they claim to be a son, an impossibility. Thus it is a negation of the worship of a son in the most eloquent form, since it is made contingent upon an impossibility. Then it negated a son in this manner by another route, namely that, since he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not worship the son, although he would have been more deserving of worshipping him if he existed, this indicates its negation. Something similar to this has been mentioned in the verse, related from Qatadah, al-Suddi, and al-Tabari.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid that the meaning is: say, if the Most Merciful had a son in your assumption, then I am the first to worship Allah alone and to deny what you say. Thus, by his, peace be upon him, being the first of the worshippers, is meant that he, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, is the first to deny this claim against them. The connection in the conditional sentence is in terms of the fact that their attribution of a son to Allah, exalted is He, requires that the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, should deny them, and be the first to reject it, because he is the bearer of the call to monotheism (*tawḥīd*). The Imam (al-Razi) was unaware of this, so he rejected the validity of this interpretation. Some have strained and said: the consequent is caused by the condition with regard to priority in worship and monotheism among them, for if they all agree on that claim, then the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, would undoubtedly be the first of them in worshipping Allah alone. It has also been said that the causal relation is in terms of informing and mentioning, like [the example]: "if you strike me, then I will not strike you," and this is better than what came before. The truth is that the connection is obscure and only appears to Mujahid. Abu Hatim related from a group, without naming any of them, that *al-ʿābidīn* derives from *ʿabida yaʿbadu* (like *faraḥa yafraḥu*), meaning "to be averse to something" when one is disgusted by it. From this is his saying:

*And I would be averse if I were to satirize Kulayb with Darim*

And another's saying:

*Whenever the close friend wills, he cuts off his companion, and becomes disgusted with him, unquestionably, while being unjust.*

That is: if the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first of those who are averse to the son, or to His being [attributed] to Allah, glorified is He, and to its attribution to Him, mighty and majestic is He. Something similar to this has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Tasti transmitted from him that Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq said to him: "Inform me about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾." He said: "I am the first to recoil from the idea that Allah, exalted is He, has a son." This interpretation is supported by the recitation of al-Sulami and al-Yamani (*al-ʿabidīn*), the plural of *ʿabid* (like *ḥadhir* and *ḥadhirīn*), which is the known meaning of "to be averse," and it is rarely said with *ʿābid* in this sense. For this reason Ibn ʿArafa weakened this interpretation, since it involves using a usage that is rarely used in their speech. Al-Khalil mentioned in *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* that it was recited as *al-ʿabdīn* with a sukun on the *bāʾ*, a lightened form of *al-ʿabidīn* with a kasra. Abu Hatim said: *al-ʿabid* with a kasra on the *bāʾ* means "one of intense anger." Abu ʿUbayda said: the Arabs say *ʿabadanī ḥaqqī*, meaning "my right denied me." It is also related from al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, Zuhayr ibn Muhammad (and this is a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas), Qatadah, and al-Suddi, also that *in* is a negative particle, meaning: "the Most Merciful had no son, so I am the first to say that, to worship, and to affirm His oneness." The *kāna* here is for continuity, and the intended meaning is the continuity of the negation, not the negation of continuity. The *fa* is causal. This was criticized as contrary to the apparent meaning, with the causal connection being obscure or of questionable merit. Makki claimed that it is not permissible, because it implies the negation of a son in the past, and "as you see, this is [unsound]."

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-Aʿmash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited, as al-Qadi said, *wuldun* with a damma on the *wāw* and a sukun on the *lām*, which is the plural of *walad* (with a fatḥa on both).

Glorified is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe (﴿سُبْحانَ رَبِّ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾). That is, above their description, or above what they describe Him as being, namely that He, glorified be He, has a son.

[Page 106]

In the addition of the name "the Lord" to the greatest and strongest of bodies (the heavens and earth) there is an indication that these, and the creatures within them, are under His sovereignty (malakut) and lordship (rububiyyah), exalted and majestic is He. How could it be imagined that any part of them could be a part of Him, glorified be He? That would contradict the necessity of existence (wujub al-wujud) for Him. In the repetition of this glorious name there is also an exaltation of the status of the Throne.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 83:

﴿So leave them﴾: leave them, turning away from them, since they did not submit to the truth after hearing this clear proof. ﴿Let them plunge﴾ into their falsehoods ﴿and play﴾ in their worldly life. What they are engaged in, of sayings and deeds, is nothing but a matter of ignorance. The verb is in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative. ﴿Until they meet their Day that they are promised﴾: according to most scholars this is the Day of Resurrection, and it is also reported from Ikrimah and a group of others that it is the Day of Badr, when they were promised destruction. Close to this is explaining it as the Day of Death. It was said: it is more appropriate to explain it as the Day of Death rather than the Day of Resurrection, because the endpoint of plunging and playing is really the Day of Death, since these end with death. The view of the majority has been defended by saying that the Day of Resurrection is the promised day, and it is called by this name in the language of the Shari'ah (revealed law). Explaining it in that other way contradicts what is well known and what follows, namely the mention of the Hour. As for the point about cessation, it is answered by saying that death and what comes after it are in the status of the Resurrection, which is why it is reported: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has come." A similar expression may be intended to indicate the length of the period, without regard to its ending, so one says: "He remains in error until the Resurrection comes."

Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin and Ubayd ibn Uqayl, from Abu 'Amr, read (﴿yalqaw﴾) as the imperfect of laqiya (to meet). It has been said that the verse is abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by the verse of the sword. ﴿And He is the One who in the heaven is God, and in the earth is God﴾: the two adverbial phrases are connected to ﴿ilah﴾ (god), because it is a descriptive noun meaning "one who is worshipped," from alaha, meaning "worshipped." It is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is God," and that is the returning pronoun of the relative clause. It is omitted because the relative clause is long, with the connection to the complement of the predicate and the conjunction following it.

Others said: the prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿ilah﴾ in view of what it indicates of the meaning of being worshipped in truth, based on its being specific to the one who is worshipped in truth. This is like the connection of a prepositional phrase to a proper name characterized by an attribute, as in your saying: "He is Hatim in Tayy, Hatim in Taghlib." On this basis the reading of Umar, Ali, Abdullah, Ubayy, al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'Ali, Bilal ibn Abi Burdah, Ibn Ya'mur, Jabir, Ibn Zayd, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Abu Shaykh al-Hunna'i, Humayd, Ibn Miqsam and Ibn al-Sumayqa' is explained: ﴿And He is the One who in the heaven is Allah, and in the earth is Allah﴾. The prepositional phrase is then connected to the proper name of majesty in view of the characteristic attribute associated with it. Some scholars considered the meaning of entitlement to worship, and gave as the reason that worship by action is not obligatory. It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase and its complement are the relative clause, and that ﴿ilah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, also, with the clause serving as an explanation (bayan, an explicative clause) of the relative clause; and that His being in the heaven is in the sense of divinity, not in the sense of residence.

It is preferred, in this case, that ﴿ilah﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject, being another predicate of the stated subject, or a substitute (badal, apposition) for the relative pronoun or for its pronoun, on the basis of allowing it. This is because the substitution of an indefinite noun that is not qualified for a definite one, when it conveys something not conveyed before, as here, is permissible and good, according to what Abu 'Ali said in al-Hujjah (his work on the readings). The explanation here is more complete and more important; for this reason it was preferred, together with what it contains of the (grammatical) estimation. In that case there is no foreign intervening element between the two coordinated items. It is not permissible for the prepositional phrase to be a fronted predicate and ﴿ilah﴾ a postponed subject, because the clause would then lack a returning pronoun, along with corrupting the meaning. The verse denies the heavenly and earthly deities and affirms divinity exclusively for Him, the Mighty and Majestic, because of what it contains of the definiteness of the two ends of the predication. The relative pronoun in such a context is like the definite article, and for the sake of giving importance to each of His divinity in the heaven and His divinity, the Mighty and Majestic, in the earth, it was said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 84:

﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth.﴾ It is not said: "He who is in the heaven and on the earth is God," nor "He who is in the heaven and the earth is God." As for the question of repetition (iʿadah), it is said that it does not apply here, because the rule is that of predominance (aghlabiyyah), as with most of the rules of Arabic grammar.

Some of the eminent scholars said: it is permissible to apply the rule here, and difference (mughayarah) between two things is more general than being so in essence (bi-l-dhat) or in attribute and consideration (bi-l-wasf wa-l-iʿtibar), and what is meant here is the second. There is no doubt that the way in which the people of the heavens worship Him, exalted is He, differs from the way in which the people of the earth worship Him, as the tracing of reports (tatabbuʿ al-athar) bears witness. So if ilah means "one worshipped" (maʿbud), the meaning of the verse is that He, exalted is He, is worshipped in the heaven in one manner and worshipped on the earth in another manner. And if it means "one bewildered about" (mutahayyar fihi), then bewilderment among the people of the heavens differs from bewilderment among the people of the earth, so necessarily their states differ from the states of the people of the earth. Among this is the difference in their knowledge: the knowledge of the people of the earth, if it is necessary (daruriyyah), is for the most part based on the senses (hiss); and if it is theoretical (nazariyyah), it is acquired through reasoning (nazar). So when the path of reasoning and the senses is blocked, they are unable and bewildered. This is not so for the people of the heavens, since they are free of acquisition and sense, so their bewilderment is of another kind. Or we may say: bewilderment in comprehending His essence and attributes, exalted is He, arises only from witnessing the signs of His greatness and the perfection of His power, exalted is He. There is no doubt that those signs in the heaven are greater than the signs on the earth. Accordingly, it is possible that ilah means "one about whom one is bewildered," and it would be a metaphor for great dignity, by way of mentioning the consequent and intending the antecedent. So the meaning would be that He, exalted is He, has great dignity in the heaven in one manner, and great dignity on the earth in another manner. End quote. This is not free of something, as is not hidden.

﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, as an indication of the negation and the exclusivity alluded to by them, for whoever is not characterized by perfect wisdom and knowledge does not deserve divinity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 85:

﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾, such as the air and the visible creatures of the atmosphere and others. ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, i.e., the knowledge of the Hour, meaning the time at which the Resurrection will take place. The verbal noun (al-masdar) is then construed with its object (idafah to the object). The Hour in its linguistic meaning (al-ma'na al-lughawi) is a small measure of time, but it is permissible that what is intended by it is its technical meaning (al-ma'na al-shar'i), which is the Day of Resurrection, and the difficulty is dissolved with the slightest reflection. In placing the predicate first there is an indication of His exclusive possession (isti'thar) of the knowledge of that, exalted is He. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ for recompense, and the shift to the second-person address is for warning (al-tahdid). Most readers recited with the ya' of the third person, and the verb in both readings is in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul). It was also read with a fatha on the ta' of the second-person address and with the active voice (al-bina' lil-fa'il). It was also read as (tuhsharun) with the ta' of the second-person address, also in the passive voice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 86:

﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession﴾, i.e., their deities whom they invoke besides Him do not possess intercession, as they claimed that they are their intercessors with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also read as (tad'una) with the second-person ta' and without the doubling (takhfif); al-Sulami and Ibn Wathhab read it with it and with the doubling of the dal. ﴿except those who bear witness to the truth﴾, which is the Tawhid (the affirmation of Allah's oneness), ﴿and they know﴾, i.e., they know it. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is restricted by it because testimony without knowledge of what is testified to is not relied upon. The pronoun is put in the plural in view of the meaning of "those" (man), just as the singular at the beginning is in view of its wording. What is meant by them are the angels, Jesus, Ezra and their likes, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them. The exception has been said to be connected if by "those whom they invoke besides Him" is meant everything that is worshipped besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and disconnected if by that is meant only the idols. It has also been said that it is wholly disconnected, and the reason given is that what is meant is the negation of the false deities' possession of intercession for the disbelievers, and whoever bears witness to the truth among them does not possess intercession for the believers. So it is as if it were said, on the assumption of generality: "And those whom they invoke besides Allah, Exalted, whatever they may be, do not possess intercession for them, but whoever bears witness to the truth possesses intercession for whomever Allah, Glorified be He, wills among the believers." So the speech is like your saying: "The people did not come to me except Zayd; he came to 'Amr." So reflect.

Mujahid and others said: What is meant by "those who bear witness to the truth" are those for whom intercession is made, and the exception on this view is connected with the omitted antecedent of the exception, as if it were said: "These angels and their likes do not possess intercession for anyone except for whoever affirmed the oneness of Allah with certainty and sincerity." 
Page 108
Similar to the omission of the antecedent of the exception is his saying:

Salim escaped, and his soul was in a narrow place, and nothing escaped except the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.
That is: nothing escaped except the sheath of a sword.

The verse has been cited as evidence that knowledge is necessary in testimony, but not in mere witnessing (mushahada).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 87:

﴿And if you ask them, "Who created them?"﴾ That is, you ask the worshippers or the worshipped. ﴿They will surely say, "Allah."﴾ Because the denial of this is impossible, due to its extreme clarity. And the manner in which the worshipped would say this is too evident to be hidden. ﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾ That is, how are they diverted from the worship of Him, exalted is He, to the worship of other than Him, glorified is He, and how do they associate others with Him, mighty and majestic is He, despite their acknowledgment that He, exalted is He, is their Creator, or despite their knowledge that their gods acknowledge this? The "fa" (then) is a consequential particle, meaning: if the matter is as such, then how, etc. The intended meaning is amazement at their associating others with Him despite this. It has also been said that the meaning is: how do they deny after their knowledge of this? So it is an expression of amazement at worshipping other than Him, exalted is He, and at their rejection of Tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), although it is innate in their nature (fitrah). In any case, it is connected to what precedes it of Tawhid and the acknowledgment that He, exalted is He, is the Creator. As for the view that the meaning is "how or where are they turned away from affirming the Resurrection, given that re-creation is easier than initial creation," and that this is connected to the matter of the Hour, as has been said, the context rejects it.

And ʿAbd al-Warith reported from Abu ʿAmr the reading (tu'fakūn) with the second-person "ta" (of address).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 88:**

﴿And [He knows] his saying, "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."﴾ With the genitive (*jarr*) on (*qīlihi*, "his saying"), and this is the reading of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Sulamī, Ibn Wathhāb, and al-Aʿmash.

al-Aʿraj, Abū Qilāba, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Muslim ibn Jundub read it with the nominative (*raf*ʿ), and this is an anomalous reading (*qirāʾa shādhdha*).

The majority (*al-jumhūr*) read it with the accusative (*naṣb*). Scholars differ on its grammatical explanation (*takhrīj*). It was said that the genitive is by coordination (*ʿaṭf*) with the word "the Hour" in His saying ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning: with Him is knowledge of His saying. The accusative is by coordination with its place (*maḥall*), since it is in the accusative position as the object of "knowledge" (*ʿilm*), which is governed by the noun it is attached to. As we mentioned earlier, it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) attached to its object, so it is as if it were said: He knows the Hour and He knows his saying. The nominative is by coordination with ﴿knowledge of the Hour﴾, with an elided noun (*ḥadhf muḍāf*); the original is "and the knowledge of his saying," the noun was elided, and the noun attached to it (the pronoun-noun) was put in its place. The first explanation is attributed to Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī), the third to Ibn Jinnī, and all of these explanations are attributed to al-Zajjāj.

The pronoun in "his saying" refers back to the Messenger (ﷺ), which is understood from His saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾. "Qīl," "qāl," and "qawl" are verbal nouns that came with one meaning. The addressed term (*munādā*) and what falls within its scope is the content of the saying. The statement comes out in the manner of regret, grief, and complaint about the unbelief of those people. Referring to them with "these" (*hāʾulāʾ*) rather than "my people" or similar expressions is a way of belittling them and disowning them because of their evil condition. The purpose of God's informing of His knowledge of that is His threat to them, glory be to Him.

It was said: the genitive is by suppressing the particle of oath (*ḥarf al-qasam*), the accusative is by omitting it and letting its verb reach it while it is elided, and the nominative is like "by your life, I will surely do." This is the view of al-Zamakhsharī, who took the saying to be "My Lord," and God's words ﴿that these...﴾ etc. to be the answer of the oath according to all three readings. The pronoun in "his saying" is as previously mentioned. The statement is then God's report that they do not believe, and His swearing by it, with the Messenger's (ﷺ) words "My Lord," to raise his status and to magnify his supplication and his turning to God, exalted is He. The "and" (*wāw*) here is for coordination, namely the coordination of the oath clause on the conditional clause. But since the oath is like a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*), the "and" has become, as it were, faded of the meaning of coordination.

In this there is the objection that the elision involved in this explanation, of expressions commonly used in oaths such as "by your life" and "by God," is clearly sound in all three readings. But in other cases, such as "his saying" here, it is not free from weakness.

It was said: the genitive is on the basis that the "and" is the "and" of oath, and the answer is omitted, meaning: "We will surely help him," or "We will surely do to them what We wish." This is reported in al-Baḥr (al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ), and it is as you see. It was said: the accusative is by coordination with the omitted object of "they write," meaning: they write their sayings and their deeds, and "his saying, My Lord, etc." And this is not worth anything.

Page 109

It was said: it is by coordination with the object of "they know," namely "the truth," meaning: they know the truth, and "his saying, etc." And this is a view that can hardly be understood.

It is reported from al-Akhfash that it is by coordination with ﴿their secret and their private counsel﴾. This was refuted on the grounds that it is not strong in meaning, together with the separation by something that does not suit being a parenthetical insertion, and with the discordance of the structure. It was objected to that the separation mentioned is clear, but as for the weakness of the meaning and the discordance of the structure, these are not accepted, because its estimated form is: "Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private counsel, and that We do not hear his saying, etc.?" This is perfectly well-ordered.

Also from him is that it is by suppressing a verb from "saying" which governs it on the basis of the verbal noun, and the estimate is "he said his saying." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: "and the Messenger said," and the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it. This was refuted on the grounds that nothing appears in it that would make it good to coordinate it with the sentence before it, and the emphasis by the verbal noun is not in its proper position, and there is no connection between ﴿so overlook﴾ and it.

The scholar al-Ṭībī, in explaining it, said: God's saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ is to be estimated as: "and We said to you: And if you were to ask them, etc.," and "you said: My Lord," in despair of their belief. The Messenger (ﷺ) was made the absent party by way of *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person), because it is as if he (ﷺ) had lost himself through grief over them, since his striving and his earnestness did not benefit them. It was said: the "and" in this view is for the circumstantial (*ḥāl*), and the statement, with "qad" estimated, is circumstantial, meaning: "then how are they turned away, while the Messenger has said: My Lord, etc.?" The summary of this is: then how are they turned away, while the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, complained of their persistence in disbelief. This is contrary to the apparent sense.

It was said: the nominative is on the basis of the inchoative (*ibtidāʾ*), and the predicate is "My Lord... they do not believe," or it is omitted, meaning "heard" or "accepted." Then the clause of the vocative and what follows it is in the position of accusative with "his saying," and the clause is circumstantial or coordinated. What is in that is not hidden.

In my opinion, the most correct view is what is attributed to al-Zajjāj. The objection to it by the separation is minor, and the objection by weakness of meaning and discordance is not accepted. In al-Kashf, after mentioning al-Zajjāj's explanation of the genitive, it is stated that the separation, namely from His saying ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ up to ﴿they are turned away﴾, is suitable as a parenthetical insertion, because His saying ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾, as is not hidden. The discourse is directed toward a severe threat expressed in His saying ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, up to His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿while they know﴾, and it is connected to His saying ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ with a connection like the staff to its jaw. His saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ is an address to whoever is able to ask, as a completion of that discourse, by their deserving what they were threatened with because of their extreme obstinacy. From this it becomes clear why the wonder appears in His saying ﴿then how are they turned away?﴾. On this basis it is clear that the connection of "and knowledge of his saying" with His saying ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ is apparent, and that the separation is connected to both with a connection that exalts its position. From this explanation it appears that what al-Zajjāj took in the three readings is good, and you may prefer it over what al-Akhfash took, by the agreement of the two readings, and because reading ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ as address turned to an unspecified addressee is more suitable to the context than reading it as address to him (ﷺ), and because it avoids supposing a saying before His saying ﴿And if you were to ask them﴾, while the context is not clearly indicative of it. End of quotation. This is the best I have seen from the exegetes on this point.

Abū Qilāba read (*yā rabba*) with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, and its explanation is clear.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 43, verse 89:**

﴿So turn away﴾ from them, meaning, ﴿turn away from them﴾, and do not hope for their faith. The original sense of ṣafḥ (turning away) is turning the side of the neck, and it is used metaphorically for turning away.

﴿And say﴾ to them, ﴿"Peace."﴾ That is, my command is "Peace," a leave-taking and a parting from you. This is not a command to greet them with salam and a greeting; it is a command to part ways. The implication is: if you refuse to accept, then my command is that I part from you. Some scholars used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of greeting non-Muslims with salam and initiating the greeting to them. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab, who said: "I was with Ali ibn Abd Allah al-Bariqi when a Jew or a Christian passed by us, and he greeted him with salam. Shu'ayb said: I said, 'He is a Jew or a Christian!' Then he recited to me the end of Surat al-Zukhruf, ﴿And [the Prophet's] saying, "O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe"﴾ to the end."

Ibn Abi Shaybah also narrated from Awn ibn Abd Allah that he said: "I said to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, 'What do you say about initiating salam to the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimma)?' He said: 'I see no harm in our initiating it to them.' I said: 'Why?' He said: 'Because of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace."﴾'" What we have mentioned shows the weakness of this argument.

Al-Suddi said: the meaning is, "Say good instead of their evil." Muqatil said: "Return to them a kindness." Al-Mawardi related: that is, "Say what will save you from their evil." All of these, as you see, are far from the truth, and the truth is what we have already presented.

﴿But they will come to know﴾ their evil state, even if that is delayed. This is a warning from Allah, glory be to Him, to them, and a consolation to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Nafi', and Hisham read ﴿تَعْلَمُونَ (you will know)﴾ with the taʾ of direct address, on the basis that it falls within the scope of "(qul)" (say). If the verse is taken to mean abstaining from fighting, then it is abrogated (mansukhah, i.e., abrogated by naskh, the principle of later revelation superseding earlier ruling). If it is taken to mean refraining from responding to them with speech, then it is not abrogated. And Allah the Most High knows best.
